The music is beautiful. It is technically accomplished. It is performed with evident care and apparent feeling. And there is something wrong with it that the party cannot immediately identify.

> *The city is full of music. You hear it before you reach the gates — a layered composition carried on the still air, string instruments weaving a melody that is complex and lovely and performed with the kind of precision that speaks of either extraordinary talent or extraordinary practice. As you enter the streets, the music separates into its component sources: a quartet performing in a small courtyard, their instruments dark-bodied and elegantly made; a solo flutist seated on a low wall, her fingers moving with the unhurried confidence of someone who has played this piece a thousand times; a choir rehearsing in an open-air theater carved into the cliff face above the market district, their voices blending in harmonics that the architecture amplifies and shapes into something richer than the voices alone could produce. The Fetchlings who pass you on the street nod pleasantly. Several pause to listen to whichever performer is nearest, their expressions appreciative, their heads tilted at the same angle, their attention held for the same duration before they move on. The music is beautiful. You listen for a long time before you realize what is wrong with it. It is the same piece. Every performer, every ensemble, every soloist you have heard since entering the city is performing the same composition — or rather, different movements of the same work, layered and distributed across the city's acoustic architecture so that a listener walking through the streets hears the full piece unfold around them in space rather than time. It is extraordinary. It is the only thing they play.*

**The Dream in Practice**

This is the party's first sustained encounter with the Dream-bound population, and the GM should use it to establish the Dream's effects through accumulation rather than exposition. The Fetchlings of Sonoria are not hostile, not evasive, and not obviously wrong. They are friendly in a measured, consistent way — the same warm greeting, the same willingness to help, the same mild interest in the party's presence that never deepens into curiosity or sharpens into suspicion. They answer questions readily. They offer directions, recommendations, and hospitality. They are pleasant company. The wrongness emerges in the details.

A musician named **Thessaly** — a Fetchling woman who performs in the central courtyard quartet — is happy to speak with the party about her work. She has been playing with this quartet for as long as she can remember. She cannot remember how long that is. When asked, she considers the question with genuine interest rather than alarm and concludes that it must be "quite some time," then moves on without apparent discomfort. She plays the compositions of a master named Orenthal, whose works she considers the finest ever produced on Nocturne. When asked about other composers, she lists several — all of them pre-curse, though she does not know this — and describes their works with evident appreciation. When asked whether any new compositions have been written recently, she pauses. The pause is the first moment of visible processing the party has seen from a Dream-bound Fetchling. She is not troubled by the question, but she cannot answer it. After a moment she says that she has been focused on refining her interpretation of Orenthal's Seventh Suite and has not had time to explore new works, and the conversation moves on. She does not notice the gap. The party should.

Other details the GM can deploy:

A concert hall that seats three hundred runs nightly performances. The program for this evening is the same program it has run every evening for five centuries, though no one in the audience knows this — the audience has died and reconstituted so many times that the performance is always, from their perspective, the first time they have heard it. Their applause is genuine. Their enthusiasm is identical each night.

A luthier's workshop contains instruments of extraordinary quality — maintained, repaired, restrung, but all of pre-curse manufacture. The luthier, **Corvo**, can discuss the properties of different tonewoods and construction techniques with expert knowledge. He has not built a new instrument in five hundred years. His workshop contains materials, tools, and empty workbenches that are kept immaculately clean. When asked about his current projects, he gestures at an instrument on his bench — a half-completed body that has been in the same state of half-completion for centuries, its progress arrested at the precise moment the Dream fell. He describes it as "coming along" and expects to finish it "when the design feels right." The design has not felt right for five hundred years.

A composer's study contains sheaves of blank manuscript paper, pots of ink, and writing instruments arranged with care. The composer — an elderly Fetchling named **Mirel** — sits at her desk each morning, considers the blank page before her, and waits for inspiration. Inspiration does not come. She finds this mildly disappointing but not distressing. She has been waiting for "quite some time" and expects a breakthrough "any day now." The blank pages in her study number in the hundreds. None of them have ever been filled.

*Detect magic* cast on any Dream-bound Fetchling reveals a transmutation/necromancy hybrid aura — faint but persistent, woven into the subject's being rather than sitting on it like a typical enchantment. *True seeing* reveals the translucent quality described in the GM Guidance: the Fetchlings appear slightly less substantial than living beings, their edges softening into faint luminescence, their physical presence ghostlike without crossing into the spectral. The effect is subtle in the valley's twilight but unmistakable under magical scrutiny.

If a party member attempts to confront a Dream-bound Fetchling directly — telling them they are cursed, showing them evidence of the repetition, pointing out the blank manuscript pages or the half-finished instrument — the response is consistent. The Fetchling listens with polite attention. They consider the party member's words with what appears to be genuine thought. Then they disagree, gently and without rancor, and offer an alternative explanation that satisfies them completely. Mirel has not written anything new because she is "between projects." Corvo's instrument has been half-finished for a long time because "good work cannot be rushed." The concert hall runs the same program because "why change what works?" The explanations are delivered with such sincerity that the party may begin to doubt their own perception. The Dream does not merely prevent the Fetchlings from seeing the truth — it provides them with a replacement truth that is, from the inside, indistinguishable from the real thing.

**The Monastery and the Old Man on the Mountain**

The Fetchlings of Sonoria do not volunteer the Old Man's existence. He is not a secret — he is simply outside the range of things the Dream-bound population finds interesting enough to mention unprompted. If the party asks the right questions, however — about the history of the valley, about anyone who might understand the broken bridge, about the "old ways" that predate the Dream — the Fetchlings' answers may include a reference to the monastery on the mountain and the old human who lives there. "He knows much about the old ways," a Fetchling might say, with the same mild tone they use for everything. "He has been there a long time. We do not visit him often." The recommendation is delivered without emphasis. The party must recognize its significance on their own.

The monastery sits on a shelf of rock above Sonoria, reached by a winding mountain path that the Dream-bound monks maintain out of habit rather than devotion. The building is old — older than the Dream, older than the cities in the valleys below — and its architecture is distinct from the Fetchling construction that characterizes the rest of Nocturne. Where the valley's buildings are elegant and acoustically refined, the monastery is simple: thick walls of undressed stone, narrow windows, a single courtyard open to the sky. It was built for contemplation rather than performance, and its position above the valley speaks of a tradition that sought distance from the world rather than engagement with it.

The monks are Fetchlings, Dream-bound like every other Kayal on Nocturne. They move through the monastery's routines with the same placid contentment the party has observed in the city below — sweeping corridors, tending a garden of plants that do not grow, performing rituals whose meaning they cannot articulate but whose forms they maintain with immaculate precision. They are friendly enough if approached, though their answers to questions about the monastery's purpose or history follow the familiar pattern of cheerful deflection. They know a man lives above them, at the shrine on the peak. They describe him as "the old teacher" and note that he has been there "for quite some time." They do not visit him. They cannot explain why.

Above the monastery, a stairway of roughly a thousand steps has been cut into the mountainside — narrow, steep, exposed to the wind, climbing from the monastery's upper courtyard to a small shrine at the summit. The stairs are ancient and worn smooth by centuries of use that ended when the Dream fell, and the climb is arduous enough that it serves as its own kind of test. The shrine at the top is the simplest structure the party has encountered on Nocturne: a single open platform of dark stone, ringed by low walls, oriented to face the eastern ridgeline where the mountains are lowest. It is the only place on Nocturne where the light of the sun touches the world. For a few minutes each day, at the hour that passes for dawn, the sun crests the ridgeline just enough to send a sliver of direct light across the shrine's platform before the mountains reclaim it. The light does not reach the valley below. It touches only this place.

The **Old Man on the Mountain** sits at the center of the shrine's platform. He is human — immediately and obviously so, the first non-Fetchling the party has encountered since arriving on Nocturne. He is old in a way that defies precise estimation, his skin weathered and dark, his hair white and wild, his frame thin but not frail. He sits cross-legged in a posture that suggests meditation, and at first glance he appears to be deep in contemplation. A closer look reveals something wrong. His eyes are not closed in peace — they are squeezed shut, the muscles of his face taut with strain. His lips move continuously, forming words too quiet to make out, and his hands — resting on his knees in what should be a position of stillness — tremble with a fine, persistent agitation. He is not meditating. He is struggling.

Nothing the party does can rouse him. Speaking to him, touching him, shaking him, casting healing magic on him — none of it produces a response beyond a momentary intensification of the muttering before he subsides back into the same agitated trance. *Detect magic* reveals a divine aura of considerable power emanating from the Old Man himself — not a spell cast upon him but something intrinsic to his nature, compressed and distorted as though something is sitting on it. *Detect evil* reveals the source: a powerful malevolent presence lurking in the immediate vicinity of the shrine, its essence wrapped around the Old Man's divine nature like a parasite feeding on a host. The presence is not visible. It is hidden — folded into the cracks in the stone, nestled in the shadows beneath the low walls, dispersed through the air around the shrine in a way that makes it difficult to localize until the party actively attempts to disrupt it.

When the party identifies and moves to disrupt the feeding — through *dispel evil*, direct magical assault on the parasitic presence, or any deliberate attempt to sever the connection between the hidden entity and the Old Man — the **Hishandura** manifests. The Asura has been lurking in a state of near-incorporeality, its essence diffused around the shrine to maximize its feeding surface, and it coalesces with a sound like stone splitting in a furnace. The stone of the shrine's platform cracks in a radial pattern centered on where the Old Man sits, as though the creature's true weight — borne across centuries in a distributed state — has suddenly concentrated in a single point. The air turns oppressive and hot, thick with the smell of something sacred being slowly consumed.

> *The shadows around the shrine gather and thicken. The stone beneath your feet cracks — a radial pattern spreading outward from the Old Man's seated figure, as though something of enormous weight has just arrived. The air, which was mountain-cold a moment ago, turns furnace-hot. And then the thing is there, filling the space between the low walls as though it has always been there and you simply could not see it. Four arms, each thicker than a man's torso. Two faces sharing a single massive head: one weeping tears that hiss where they strike the cracked stone, the other bared in a rictus of contempt that never changes. It crouches over the Old Man the way a predator crouches over a kill it does not intend to share.*
>
> *The weeping face speaks first. "More pilgrims." The snarling face finishes the thought. "The road is open, then. We wondered when."*

The Hishandura — born from champions wrongfully abandoned by their gods, as all Hishanduras are — was sent to Nocturne centuries ago by the Asura hierarchy to neutralize the Old Man before he could fulfill his purpose. It has done so with patient, methodical cruelty: not killing him, which would release his essence and allow the gods to send another, but feeding on him slowly, draining his power just enough to keep him helpless while keeping him alive enough to sustain the feeding. The Asura considers this arrangement elegant. It has had five hundred years to develop opinions about the gods, about divine purpose, about the arrogance of sending a single messenger to fix a broken world, and it will share these opinions with the party at length if permitted. It is not stalling — it genuinely enjoys the conversation. It has not had anyone to talk to in a very long time.

The fight takes place on the exposed platform of the shrine — open to the sky and the wind, with the thousand-step stairway as the only exit and the Old Man seated at the center of the cracked stone. The Hishandura's Destructive Blades ability allows it to ignore hardness on the shrine's low walls and the stone platform itself, and it will use this to shatter cover and collapse sections of the stairway's upper reaches if the party attempts to retreat. Its Repentant Rain — the spray of gore that blinds nearby enemies after a critical hit — is effective on the open platform, where the 30-foot cone can catch multiple party members at once. The Hishandura fights with the savagery of a creature defending a food source it has held for centuries, and it does not retreat willingly. It must be destroyed or driven from the shrine by force.

*GM note: The Hishandura stat block is already in the appendix (see Stat Block Appendix, Hishandura entry). The encounter should be challenging but not overwhelming for a level 16 mythic tier 7 party — the Hishandura is CR 15, which means it is a meaningful threat that can punish poor tactics without being a potential party-killer. The real danger is the Old Man: he sits at the center of the platform, unable to move, and if the party uses area-effect abilities without care they risk killing him. The Old Man has 1 hp and no defensive capabilities in his current state. Any area damage that reaches him will kill him. If the Old Man is killed, his divine essence disperses — the information and guidance he provides (see below) would be lost for this chapter. The party can still complete Nocturne without the Old Man's help, but they will lack the structural briefing about the bridges, the orbs, and the spirits, and — critically — they will not receive the Tamaron clue. The GM should make the Old Man's fragile state apparent to observant players (Perception DC 12 to notice his agitated state and the way the Hishandura's feeding is visibly draining him) and let the party make tactical choices accordingly.*

**The Old Man's Guidance**

When the Hishandura is destroyed or driven off, the change in the Old Man is not gradual — the parasitic feeding stops, and the divine essence that has been compressed for centuries begins to reassert itself. The agitation drains from his face. His muttering stops. His hands still. He opens his eyes — clear, sharp, irritable — and looks at the party with the expression of a man who has been interrupted during something important and is not yet certain whether the interruption was worth the bother.

The Old Man is not grateful, or if he is, he expresses it in the manner of someone who considers gratitude a waste of time when there is work to be done. His first words are a gruff acknowledgment — "Took your time" — followed by a demand to know who the party is and what they are doing on Nocturne. He listens to their answer with visible impatience, interrupting when they provide details he considers irrelevant and snapping his fingers when they pause too long between sentences. He is crabby, dismissive, and entirely lacking in the solemn gravitas that divine messengers are supposed to project. He refers to Baselia as "that young fool" and the Dream-bound population as "those idiots," and his assessment of the situation — delivered while poking at a crack in the shrine's stone with one bony finger — carries the exasperated tone of a man who saw the catastrophe coming, was unable to prevent it, and has spent five centuries being proven right in the most unpleasant way possible.

The Old Man is a being similar in nature to the Nexian Oracle — not a mortal, not a god, but something intrinsic to the world itself, a part of Nocturne the way the Oracle is a part of Nexus. He has existed on this mountain since before the Dream fell, since before the Cabal, since before the ten heroes first walked the Rainbow Road. Where the Oracle speaks in riddles and pronouncements shaped by her nature as a conduit of mythic power, the Old Man speaks plainly, and his plainness is its own form of authority. He does not need to be mysterious. He has been watching this world destroy itself for five hundred years and he has no patience left for circumlocution.

What the Old Man tells the party, delivered in a stream of clipped, irritable sentences punctuated by dismissive gestures:

The Dream is a curse. "Those idiots" — the Fetchlings — cannot see it because the curse was designed that way. The Cabal sorcerers who twisted Baselia's spell were corrupted by powers older and more deliberate than anything the sorcerers themselves understood, and the curse they created serves purposes beyond the merely local. The population is trapped between life and death, cannot create, and reconstitutes without memories when killed. The Old Man does not belabor these points — if the party has spent any time in the valley below, they have seen the effects firsthand. He is more interested in what they have not yet learned.

The five valleys were connected by light bridges powered by orbs of concentrated magical energy. The Cabal spirits — the ghosts of the sorcerers Baselia hunted down and killed — hold the orbs in strongholds across the five valleys. The bridges are broken because the spirits want them broken: isolation serves the curse, and the curse serves the demons who corrupted the Cabal in the first place. The party must reclaim the orbs and restore the bridges to reach the Citadel of Lament at the center of the world. "That young fool" — Baselia — is there, and she has been there for five centuries, making everything worse. Each spirit is different and must be handled differently. The Old Man does not elaborate on the specifics of spirits two through five — "You'll figure it out, or you won't" — but he provides pointed guidance about the first: "The musician. She remembers what she lost. That is her weakness and her weapon. Do not fight her if you can help it."

If Tamaron was turned on Illium, the Old Man addresses this with characteristic bluntness. He tells the party that Baselia cannot be reached by force alone — "not because she is strong, though she is, but because the thing that is destroying her is grief, and you cannot punch grief in the face." The man she loved is the only person who can stand in front of her and make her stop. "Bring him. When the way is open, bring him. He will not want to come. He will come anyway, because he owes her that much, and because the fool still loves her, even after everything."

If Tamaron was killed, the Old Man's response is shorter and harder. He closes his eyes for a moment — the only sign of emotion the party sees from him — and says, "Then she is lost. You will have to fight her. She will not make it easy, and she will not thank you for the mercy." He does not elaborate. There is nothing to elaborate on.

The Old Man may answer a few additional questions if the party approaches him with deference — he responds to respect, grudgingly, though he has no patience for flattery or lengthy preambles. Questions about the nature of the Dream, the Cabal's history, the structure of the valleys, or the Old Man's own nature are met with terse, accurate answers. Questions he considers stupid — "Can we break the curse by killing all the Fetchlings?" — are met with a stare that could curdle milk, followed by a silence that makes the asker wish they had not spoken. When he decides the interview is over — and the decision is his, not the party's — he waves one hand in a gesture of dismissal that is simultaneously rude and effective. The party finds themselves standing in the monastery's courtyard, the thousand-step stairway above them, the shrine invisible from this angle. If they climb back up, the Old Man is gone. The shrine is empty, the cracked stone the only evidence that anything happened there.

*GM note: The Old Man is an optional encounter — the party is not directed to him by any mandatory plot event, and a group that does not explore the monastery or ask the right questions in Sonoria may miss him entirely. This is intentional. The chapter can be completed without his guidance: the party can discover the bridge/orb/spirit structure through direct experience, and the Tamaron dependency has been hinted at through the Chapter 9 transition and through turned Warlock dialogue. What the Old Man provides is clarity — he accelerates the party's understanding and, crucially, delivers the Tamaron clue in its most direct form. A party that misses the Old Man will take longer to piece together what they need to do and may not realize that Tamaron is Baselia's lever until it is too late to easily recruit him. The GM should make the Old Man findable — the Fetchlings' recommendation, if prompted, is genuine and useful — but should not force the encounter. The Old Man should be played as written: gruff, crabby, impatient, dismissive, and absolutely reliable. His information is correct. His assessment of the situation is accurate. His personality is insufferable. These things are not in conflict.*

*One additional note: if the party frees the Old Man, the timing of the Hishandura's destruction should coincide with Nocturne's brief dawn — the few minutes when the sun crests the eastern ridgeline and touches the shrine — this is the only spot on this world the sun ever touches. The light that falls on the platform after the fight is the first direct sunlight the Old Man has felt in five centuries, and though he does not comment on it, the GM should describe it: a narrow band of golden light crossing the cracked stone, warming the Old Man's face as he opens his eyes for the first time since the Asura found him. It is a small moment. It should feel like a large one.*

---

### Scene 3: Stronghold 1 — The Negotiator

The first stronghold sits at the valley's far end, built into the cliff face above the broken light bridge — a structure that was once a concert hall and has become, over five centuries, something between a prison and a reliquary. The architecture is Nocturne's acoustic style taken to its most extreme expression: the entire structure is a single vast resonance chamber carved into the living rock, its walls shaped to capture sound and hold it, its corridors and galleries arranged so that a note struck at the entrance carries to the innermost chamber without losing clarity or force. Before the Dream, this was the Valley of Music's greatest performance space — a hall where a solo instrument could fill a room the size of a cathedral, where the acoustics were so precisely calibrated that an audience of a thousand could hear a whispered phrase from the stage. Now it is the domain of the first Cabal spirit, and the sound it holds is not music but the echo of everything the spirit remembers and cannot stop remembering.

The approach is not hidden. The stronghold's entrance is a grand arch cut into the cliff face, flanked by carved pillars whose surfaces depict musicians in performance — the figures frozen mid-note, their instruments raised, their postures alive with a motion the stone cannot complete. The arch opens into a corridor that descends at a gentle grade into the mountain, the walls smooth and acoustically treated, the ambient sound changing as the party moves deeper: the wind from the valley mouth gives way to silence, and the silence gives way to something else. Music. Faint, distant, achingly beautiful — a solo string instrument playing a melody the party has not heard before, its tone rich and sorrowful and technically accomplished in a way that suggests a performer of extraordinary skill. The melody does not repeat. It develops, shifts, explores variations on its theme, moves through passages of complexity and passages of stark simplicity with the confidence of a musician who has had centuries to refine every phrase. The sound grows clearer as the party descends. It is coming from the heart of the stronghold.

The interior of the concert hall has been transformed by centuries of the spirit's occupation. The original performance space — a vast oval chamber with tiered seating carved into the walls, a central stage of polished dark stone, and a domed ceiling whose curve was calculated to project sound evenly across every seat — is intact, but its character has changed. The seats are empty. The stage is occupied by a single figure. The walls, which were once bare stone shaped for acoustic perfection, are now covered in writing — musical notation, scratched into the rock with something sharp, covering every surface from floor to ceiling in a dense, obsessive hand. Thousands of compositions. Tens of thousands of measures. The spirit has been writing music on the walls of her prison for five hundred years, and the walls are nearly full.

**Serenica** — the spirit's name, or the name she held when she was alive — manifests as a translucent Fetchling woman whose appearance shifts between two states: the young musician she was before the Cabal, and the hollow-eyed sorcerer she became after. The shifts are involuntary and frequent, her form flickering between the two like a candle in a draft, and she is aware of them in a way that clearly causes her distress. She holds an instrument — a stringed thing of dark wood and silver wire that exists in the same spectral state she does, neither fully present nor fully absent — and she has been playing it since the party first heard her from the corridor. She stops when she sees them. The silence that follows is the loudest thing in the room.

Serenica does not attack. She watches the party enter with an expression that cycles through surprise, suspicion, calculation, and something that might be hope before settling into careful neutrality. She is the most coherent of the five Cabal spirits — the one who retains the largest share of who she was before the curse, before the Asura corruption, before the desperate pact with dark powers that she entered believing it would make her art transcend mortal limitations. She remembers what she did. She remembers why she did it. She remembers what it cost her. The other spirits have fragmented in various ways — madness, rage, obsession — but Serenica's curse is clarity. She sees herself and her situation with agonizing precision, and she has had five centuries to sit with that vision in a concert hall designed to make every sound resonate.

> *The spirit stands at the center of a stage built for orchestras. She is alone. The instrument in her hands is a thing of silver wire and dark wood that flickers in and out of solidity the way she does — present, then translucent, then present again, as though neither the instrument nor the woman holding it can decide whether they exist. The walls around her are covered in notation. You can see it clearly in the faint luminescence that clings to her form: measures, staves, dynamic markings, annotations in a hand that started precise and grew more desperate as the available stone diminished. There is music on every surface. On the ceiling. On the backs of the stone seats. On the floor of the stage itself, written around her feet in a spiral that tightens toward the center.*
>
> *She looks at you the way a prisoner looks at a door that has opened for the first time in memory — with an intensity that is not quite hope and not quite fear but something between them that has no comfortable name.*
>
> *"You can hear it," she says. It is not a question. "The music. You can hear it." Her voice resonates in the chamber's perfect acoustics, every harmonic preserved, every overtone sustained. "The others cannot. The Dream-bound come to the door sometimes. They stand there and they listen and they hear nothing. Five hundred years of composition and the only audience I have is the stone."*

**The Negotiation**

Serenica does not want to fight and will not initiate combat unless the party forces the issue. She holds the Valley 1 orb — it rests in a cradle of silver wire on the stage behind her, pulsing with the concentrated magical energy that once powered the light bridge — and she is willing to give it up. She has been willing to give it up for centuries. The orb is not what keeps her here. What keeps her here is the binding — the same curse that created the Dream also bound the Cabal spirits to their strongholds, and Serenica cannot leave the concert hall any more than the Dream-bound Fetchlings can leave their hollow routines. The orb is a prison key she holds but cannot use on her own door.

What Serenica wants is to be free. Not freed from the stronghold in a tactical sense — she is not asking the party to break down a wall or dispel a ward — but freed from the binding that ties her essence to this place. She has spent five centuries studying the nature of her imprisonment with the same obsessive precision she once brought to composition, and she understands its structure better than any living mortal could. The binding is threaded through the stronghold's acoustic architecture — the same properties that make the concert hall a perfect resonance chamber also make it a perfect cage, the curse using the building's own design to contain the spirit within it. Serenica can describe the binding's structure in exhaustive technical detail to any party member capable of understanding magical theory (Knowledge: Arcana DC 15 to follow her explanation). She cannot break it herself. The binding requires an act of external will — a *dispel magic* at CL 20, a *break enchantment* at CL 18, a *wish* or *miracle*, or a targeted *mythic dispelling* using the party's mythic power. Any of these releases her. She dissipates — not destroyed but unbound, her essence free to pass on to whatever awaits dead sorcerers who made pacts with powers they should not have trusted. She considers this outcome acceptable. Five hundred years of clarity have given her time to make her peace with oblivion.

The negotiation should feel like a conversation with a person, not a puzzle with a solution. Serenica is intelligent, articulate, and genuinely desperate in a way she works hard to conceal. She has been alone for five centuries with nothing but her own music and her own memories, and the party's arrival is the first meaningful event in her existence since the curse fell. She will not beg. She will not threaten. She will explain her situation with the measured composure of someone who has rehearsed this conversation a thousand times in her head and is now, at last, having it with real people. She answers questions about the other spirits, the bridges, the orbs, and the Dream with the same forthright precision — she has no reason to lie and no interest in games. She wants one thing, and the party can give it to her, and if they choose to do so she will give them the orb and whatever information she possesses and then she will be gone.

If the party does not have the magical capability to break the binding — possible but unlikely at this level — Serenica accepts this with visible disappointment that she immediately suppresses. She offers the orb anyway, in exchange for something smaller: new music. She has not heard a genuinely new composition in five hundred years. The Dream-bound cannot create; the Asuras have no interest in art; and her own works, however numerous, are all products of the same mind and the same five centuries of isolation. If a party member can perform something she has never heard — a song from another world, a melody learned in a tavern on Nexus, a hymn from a faith she does not know — she will listen with an attention so total and so hungry that it borders on frightening. The performance does not need to be skilled. It needs to be new. A Perform check is appropriate (DC 10 — the threshold is low because the quality matters less than the novelty), and even a mediocre performance of an unfamiliar tune draws from Serenica a response that is the most genuine emotion the party has seen on Nocturne: she closes her eyes, and for a moment her form stops flickering and holds steady, and the expression on her face is one of such acute, devastating gratitude that it is difficult to watch.

She gives the orb freely in either case. If the binding is broken, she hands it to the party with a steadiness that does not waver, says nothing that resembles a farewell, and dissipates. If the binding remains, she sets the orb on the edge of the stage and returns to her instrument, and as the party leaves the concert hall they hear her playing again — the melody they performed for her, transposed and elaborated, already becoming something new under her hands. The sound follows them up the corridor and fades only when they reach the open air.

A third option exists, though Serenica does not offer it: the party can simply ask for the orb. If they explain what they are doing — restoring the bridges, reaching the Citadel, confronting Baselia — Serenica listens with the same careful attention she brings to everything and gives the orb over without demanding anything in return. "Take it," she says. "If you can do what you say you can do, then the orb does more good in your hands than it does sitting on my stage." This option is the least satisfying for Serenica — she gains nothing — but she is not so selfish as to withhold the means of her world's salvation in exchange for personal benefit. She is a sorcerer who made catastrophic choices out of artistic ambition. She is not a monster.

**The Failure State**

If the party chooses to fight — if they refuse to negotiate, attack on sight, or behave in a way that convinces Serenica they cannot be reasoned with — she defends herself. The concert hall's acoustics become weapons: Serenica's magic is sound-based, her spells manifesting as frequencies that shatter stone, burst blood vessels, and induce disorientation through subsonic vibrations that the body feels before the ears register. She is CR 16 — a dangerous opponent in her own domain, where the architecture amplifies her abilities and the enclosed space makes her area-effect attacks difficult to avoid. She fights with the ferocity of someone who has nothing left to lose and the precision of someone who has spent five centuries studying the acoustics of the room she fights in. She knows every resonant frequency, every dead spot, every angle at which sound reflects and concentrates. The party is fighting a musician in a concert hall she has had five hundred years to learn.

The GM should not make this fight easy, but neither should it be a punishment for choosing violence. Some parties will not trust the spirit. Some parties will have been attacked by enough apparently-reasonable NPCs in this campaign that they shoot first and negotiate never. The consequence of fighting Serenica is not mechanical difficulty — it is the knowledge, acquired after the fight when the party finds the walls covered in five hundred years of original composition, that they killed someone who was still creating. In a world where creation has been obliterated, Serenica was the only being on Nocturne still producing something new. That should sit with the party whether the GM comments on it or not.

The orb is recovered either way — it sits on the stage, inert once Serenica is destroyed, and can be taken without further obstacle.

**Restoring the First Bridge**

The light bridge's pylon stands at the edge of the chasm at the valley's far end — a slender column of dark stone rising from the cliff face, its surface carved with channels and conduits that once carried the orb's energy across the span. The housing at the pylon's crown is empty, a socket of polished stone shaped to receive the orb. When the party seats the orb in its housing, the effect is immediate and spectacular.

> *The orb settles into the socket with a sound like a bell struck underwater — deep, resonant, felt in the chest rather than heard in the ears. The carved channels in the pylon's surface ignite. Light races down the stone in branching lines, tracing a pattern that was invisible before and is now unmistakable: a schematic of the bridge itself, drawn in concentrated radiance along the pylon's full height. The light reaches the base of the pylon and leaps — a single blazing ribbon of energy that arcs across the chasm, hanging in the air for a breathless moment before it stabilizes, widening, solidifying, the ribbon becoming a span, the span becoming a surface, the surface becoming a bridge of pure light that connects the two cliff faces across a darkness that has held them apart for five centuries.*
>
> *The bridge hums. The sound it produces is a sustained harmonic that the valley's acoustic architecture catches and amplifies, carrying it down into the city below. In Sonoria, Fetchlings pause in mid-step. Musicians lower their instruments. Heads turn toward the valley's edge, toward the source of a sound that none of them have heard before — genuinely, for the first time, a new sound on Nocturne. They stare. They do not understand what they are hearing or seeing. But something in the light, in the harmonic, in the sheer fact of change in a world where nothing has changed for five centuries, reaches past the Dream and touches something underneath.*
>
> *They stare for a long time. Then the moment passes, and they return to what they were doing, and the bridge blazes on above the chasm like a scar of light in the perpetual twilight.*

The party can cross. The second valley — the Valley of Literature — is visible on the far side, its lights fainter than Sonoria's, its architecture denser, the shapes of its buildings suggesting a city built around different priorities. The bridge is solid beneath the party's feet, warm to the touch, and wide enough for three abreast. It does not sway. Looking down reveals the chasm — a depth that the bridge's light does not reach, a blackness that swallows illumination without returning it. The crossing takes several minutes. On the far side, the second valley opens before them, and the second stronghold waits.

*GM note: The restoration of the first bridge is the chapter's first major turning point and should be played with appropriate weight. It is the first visible, tangible act of healing the party has performed on Nocturne — and unlike the turning of Warlocks on previous worlds, which affected individual beings, this is infrastructure. The bridge is a physical connection between places that have been severed for centuries, and its restoration produces an effect that the entire population of the valley can perceive, even if the Dream prevents them from understanding it. The Fetchlings' momentary pause — the flicker of awareness that something has changed — is the first crack in the Dream's hold. It will not break the curse. But it is the beginning of the process that may, and the party should feel the significance of that beginning. If Serenica was freed rather than destroyed, the bridge's harmonic carries a quality that the party may recognize: it sounds, faintly but unmistakably, like her music.*

---

### Scene 4: The Valley of Literature and Stronghold 2 — The Labyrinth of Knowledge

The second valley is narrower than the first, its walls steeper, the quality of the twilight darker — less violet, more grey, as though the mountains that frame it admit less of Nocturne's ambient light. Where Sonoria was built for sound, the city in this valley was built for silence. The architecture is dense, inward-facing, constructed around enclosed courtyards and covered walkways that muffle ambient noise rather than amplifying it. The buildings are taller than Sonoria's — five and six stories of dark stone, their facades punctuated by narrow windows designed to admit light while excluding distraction. Every major structure the party can see from the valley rim has the same fundamental character: thick walls, small openings, an interior orientation that prizes the controlled environment over the open air. This is a city of rooms. Reading rooms, writing rooms, lecture halls, private studies, archival vaults. The city is called **Lexara** in the oldest records, though like Sonoria's residents, the Dream-bound Fetchlings who live here have forgotten the name and simply call it "the city."

The streets of Lexara are quieter than Sonoria's — the music that defined the first valley is absent here, replaced by a low murmur of voices that the party hears as they descend into the city proper. The Fetchlings of Lexara talk. They talk constantly, earnestly, with the focused energy of people engaged in work they consider vital. Conversations overlap in the covered walkways and spill from open doorways: debates, lectures, recitations, close readings of texts conducted with the intensity of surgery. The city is not silent in practice — it is silent in architecture, its buildings designed to contain and direct the sound of discourse rather than eliminate it. Every public space has the acoustics of a seminar room. Every private study has walls thick enough to seal out the world. Lexara was built by people who believed that the life of the mind required physical infrastructure as deliberate as any concert hall, and the infrastructure remains immaculate even though the minds it serves have been frozen for five centuries.

> *The city is full of voices. Not loud — the architecture does not permit loudness — but present, layered, coming from every direction in a murmur that resolves, as you move deeper into the streets, into distinct conversations. A group of Fetchlings stands in a covered courtyard, arranged in a loose circle, their postures alert and engaged. One speaks with precise, measured emphasis while the others listen with expressions of focused attention. Another courtyard holds a single Fetchling seated on a raised platform, reading aloud from a heavy book to an audience of twelve who take no notes but nod at irregular intervals. A third space — a long gallery whose walls are lined with shelves — contains a dozen Fetchlings moving between the shelves and a central table where manuscripts are laid out for comparison, their fingers tracing lines of text with the unhurried care of scholars who have all the time in the world.*
>
> *The voices carry a quality you have heard before. In Sonoria it was the music — technically perfect, emotionally present, and somehow wrong. Here it is the arguments. The debate in the first courtyard is passionate and articulate and both sides are making points you can follow even without context. The lecturer's reading is expressive and well-paced. The scholars at the manuscript table murmur observations to one another that sound insightful and precise. There is nothing wrong with any of it except that you have the growing suspicion — confirmed, when you listen long enough, by the repetition of a particular phrase, a particular rhetorical turn, a particular citation — that you are hearing the same conversations this city has been having for five hundred years.*

**The Dream Deepened**

The Valley of Literature provides the party's second sustained encounter with the Dream, and the GM should use it to deepen the horror through a different lens than the first valley's. Where Sonoria demonstrated the Dream's effect on individual creativity — the composer who cannot compose, the luthier who cannot finish — Lexara demonstrates its effect on collective intellectual life. The Fetchlings here do not create new works; they also do not generate new ideas, new interpretations, new arguments, or new questions. The entire apparatus of literary and scholarly culture — the debates, the lectures, the close readings, the archival work — continues to function with technical proficiency while producing nothing. It is a university that has been running for five centuries without advancing a single field by a single step.

A debate society meets in the largest covered courtyard every third day. The topic is always different — drawn from a rotating list of subjects established before the curse — and the participants argue with genuine conviction, marshaling evidence, constructing counterarguments, appealing to precedent and principle with rhetorical skill that would be impressive in any context. The debates never reach a conclusion. Not because the arguments are evenly matched, though they often are, but because the debaters cannot synthesize the arguments into anything new. Each side states its position, responds to the other's points, and the exchange continues until the allotted time expires, at which point the participants thank one another cordially and disperse until the next session. None of them remembers the previous debate on the same topic. The debate society has been cycling through the same list of subjects for five centuries, reaching the same impasses, deploying the same arguments, and dispersing with the same cordial satisfaction each time.

The great library of Lexara occupies the valley's largest structure — a building of seven stories, its interior a single open atrium surrounded by tiered galleries of shelves, with reading alcoves cut into the walls at every level and a cataloging desk at the ground floor staffed by a team of archivists who maintain the collection with obsessive precision. The library's catalog is a masterwork of organization: every text cross-referenced, every manuscript dated and attributed, every copy checked against every other copy for textual variants. The archivists can locate any work in the collection within minutes and discuss its provenance, its relationship to other texts, and its place in Nocturne's literary tradition with genuine expertise. The library has no acquisitions section. There is a desk for it — clearly labeled, fully equipped with intake forms and classification tools — but the forms are blank and the tools are unused. The chief archivist, a meticulous Fetchling named **Caelan**, describes the acquisitions desk as "temporarily quiet" and expects new submissions "when the current generation of writers finishes their work." There is no current generation of writers. There has not been one for five centuries. Caelan finds this fact unremarkable.

A lecturer named **Vareth** delivers a weekly public reading in one of the city's smaller halls — a close analysis of a pre-curse epic poem, conducted over the course of a year-long cycle that begins again each time it ends. His audience attends faithfully and finds each session illuminating. Vareth's analysis is genuinely brilliant — his observations about the poem's structure, its use of metaphor, its relationship to the historical events it describes are the kind of insights that emerge from deep, repeated engagement with a text over a lifetime of study. The analysis has not changed in five centuries. Vareth delivers the same insights in the same order with the same intonation each cycle, and his audience — reconstituted so many times that they have no memory of previous cycles — responds with the same appreciation each time. If a party member attends a session and later asks Vareth whether he has considered a different interpretation — any interpretation, of any aspect of the poem — Vareth listens with genuine interest, considers the suggestion with visible thought, and then steers the conversation back to his established analysis with the unconscious ease of a stream finding its accustomed channel. He does not reject the new idea. He simply cannot hold it.

*GM note: The Valley of Literature should feel like a different kind of tragedy than the Valley of Music. Sonoria's horror was intimate — the composer alone with blank pages, the luthier frozen mid-project. Lexara's horror is institutional. The machinery of intellectual life is running perfectly: the debates are vigorous, the library is immaculate, the lectures are well-attended. The output is zero. The distinction matters because it reveals a different facet of the Dream's cruelty. In Sonoria, the Dream took creativity from individuals. In Lexara, it took progress from a civilization. A single composer who cannot write is a personal tragedy. A university that cannot advance knowledge is an existential one. The party should leave Lexara understanding that the Dream did not merely freeze individual Fetchlings — it froze the capacity for cultural change itself.*

**Stronghold 2 — The Scholar's Labyrinth**

The second stronghold is embedded in the valley wall at Lexara's northern edge, its entrance an archway framed by carved stone tablets whose inscriptions shift when observed from different angles — not an illusion but a property of the stone itself, altered by the spirit within to display different texts depending on the reader's position, the ambient light, and factors the stone does not explain. The archway leads into a structure that was, before the spirit claimed it, a repository — a deep-mountain archive built to preserve Nocturne's most important texts in a controlled environment of constant temperature, low humidity, and absolute darkness. The spirit has transformed it into something else entirely. The archive's original organization — orderly, logical, designed for efficient retrieval — has been replaced by a structure that obeys a different kind of logic: the logic of a brilliant mind that has lost its grip on the distinction between knowledge and obsession.

The spirit of the second stronghold is called **Margolan**, and he was, in life, the most celebrated scholar of his generation — a polymath whose mastery ranged across history, philosophy, linguistics, and magical theory with an ease that his contemporaries found either inspiring or infuriating depending on their proximity to his ego. He joined the Cabal not for power in the martial sense but for access: the Cabal's sorcerers worked with forces that operated outside conventional magical theory, and Margolan wanted to understand them with the same completeness he brought to every other subject he studied. The Asura influence that corrupted the Cabal reached him through his defining characteristic — his need to know everything — and twisted it into something recursive and consuming. Margolan no longer seeks knowledge to understand the world. He seeks knowledge to construct a world that conforms to his understanding. The labyrinth he has built from the archive's bones is the physical expression of this: a space where the environment itself is organized by intellectual principle, where rooms rearrange themselves based on the validity of propositions stated within them, where doors open to correct answers and close to incorrect ones, and where the distinction between a test of knowledge and a prison of knowledge has been thoroughly erased.

> *The archive's corridors do not behave as corridors should. The first passage is straight and stone-walled, lined with shelves that hold books in languages you recognize and languages you do not. The second passage is not where the first suggested it would be — the turn you expected opens instead into a high-ceilinged chamber whose walls are covered in questions. Not carved, not painted — the questions exist in the stone itself, surfacing and submerging like text in water, some legible for only a moment before they sink and are replaced by others. The questions are in every language represented on the shelves. Some are simple. Some are not. One, near the floor, written in a hand that trembles at the edges, reads: "What is the difference between remembering and being unable to forget?"*

**The Challenge**

The labyrinth is primarily a skill challenge rather than a combat encounter. Margolan does not fight the party directly — he has no interest in physical confrontation, and the five centuries of incorporeal existence have left him poorly equipped for it in any case. His weapon is the labyrinth itself: a structure designed to test, confound, and ultimately trap anyone who enters it through intellectual means. The party must navigate the labyrinth to reach the central chamber where the orb is held, and navigation requires engaging with the labyrinth's logic rather than attempting to bypass it.

The labyrinth's architecture responds to knowledge. Rooms rearrange themselves based on answers given to questions posed by the walls, the floor, the doors, and — occasionally — Margolan's disembodied voice, which drifts through the passages with the distracted tone of a lecturer who has forgotten he has an audience and is speaking mainly for his own benefit. The questions range across disciplines: history, magical theory, philosophy, natural science, theology, and subjects specific to Nocturne's culture and the Nine Worlds' cosmology. The party does not need to answer every question correctly — the labyrinth is navigable through a combination of knowledge, deduction, and persistence — but correct answers open shorter paths, reveal hidden passages, and disable traps, while incorrect answers close routes, trigger defensive mechanisms, and rearrange the labyrinth in ways that increase the distance between the party and the orb.

The GM should structure the labyrinth as a series of chambers, each presenting a distinct challenge:

**The Hall of Propositions.** The first major chamber contains three doors, each inscribed with a proposition. The propositions are presented as absolute statements — "All curses can be broken by the power that created them," "The dead cannot create," "Memory is the foundation of identity" — and the party must choose which door to pass through. There is no objectively correct answer. Each door leads to a different path through the labyrinth, and the path's character reflects the proposition chosen: the "curses" door leads through chambers focused on magical theory, the "dead" door through chambers focused on the nature of the Dream, and the "memory" door through chambers focused on history and identity. All three paths reach the center eventually. The choice determines what the party encounters along the way and what kind of knowledge is tested.

**The Shifting Archives.** A series of rooms whose shelves contain texts that rearrange themselves when the party enters. Each room poses a research problem — a question that can be answered by finding the correct text on the correct shelf and identifying the relevant passage. The texts are real (drawn from Nocturne's literary tradition) and the questions are genuine; this is a library challenge in the most literal sense. Knowledge (History) DC 18, Knowledge (Arcana) DC 16, and Linguistics DC 15 checks allow the party to locate and interpret the relevant texts. Failure does not prevent progress but triggers the room's defensive mechanism: the shelves begin to close inward, compressing the space and forcing the party to solve the problem under time pressure or find the exit before the room contracts to a size that causes harm (Reflex DC 16 to escape, 4d6 bludgeoning damage on failure).

**The Debate Chamber.** A round room with two podiums facing each other. Margolan's voice fills the space — not hostile but genuinely engaged — and poses a philosophical question to the party. He wants to argue. Not to defeat the party, but because he has not had a real intellectual exchange in five centuries and the prospect is irresistible to him, even now, even in his diminished and obsessive state. The party must engage him in structured debate: state a position, support it with argument, respond to his counterarguments. Diplomacy DC 18 or Knowledge (Philosophy/History/Arcana) DC 20 to construct an argument that Margolan finds intellectually satisfying. If the party makes a genuinely novel point — something Margolan has not considered in five centuries of solitary thought — his voice goes silent for a long moment before the door to the next chamber opens on its own. If the party refuses to engage or attempts to bypass the chamber, the exits seal and the room begins to fill with a fine dust that obscures vision and imposes increasing penalties to concentration (Fort DC 14 each round, cumulative -1 to Intelligence and Wisdom-based checks on failure). The dust clears when the party engages with the debate.

**The Final Passage.** The corridor leading to the central chamber is lined with the spirit's own writing — not the obsessive notation of Serenica's walls but dense, tightly argued prose covering every surface, a philosophical treatise that Margolan has been composing since his death. The treatise concerns the nature of consciousness, memory, and the relationship between knowledge and existence — and it is, despite its author's madness, genuinely brilliant. A party member who reads closely (Linguistics DC 14 or Knowledge: Arcana DC 16) recognizes that the treatise contains, buried in its dense argumentation, a precise and accurate description of the Dream's mechanism — how the curse works, what sustains it, and why the population cannot perceive it. This information is valuable: it provides a +2 circumstance bonus to any future attempt to dispel or weaken the Dream's effects, and it confirms (for a party that has not spoken with the Old Man) the structural details about the bridges, the orbs, and the spirits' role in maintaining the curse. Margolan embedded this information deliberately. He understood the curse better than any other being on Nocturne, and he wrote it down where someone capable of following his argument might find it.

**The Central Chamber and the Orb**

The labyrinth's center is a single circular room, smaller than expected, its walls bare of text for the first time since the party entered the stronghold. The orb sits on a stone pedestal at the room's center, its light the only illumination — a steady, warm glow that contrasts sharply with the spectral flicker of the labyrinth's ambient luminescence. Margolan's spirit manifests here for the first and only time: a translucent figure seated in a chair that does not exist, his posture that of a man reading a book he holds in hands that pass through one another when he forgets to concentrate on maintaining his form. He is gaunt, distracted, and visibly frayed — the five centuries of solitary intellectual labor have worn his coherence thinner than Serenica's, and his presence flickers with an instability that suggests he is not far from dissolution regardless of what the party does.

Margolan does not fight for the orb. He does not bargain for it. He looks up when the party enters, studies them with an expression that is equal parts curiosity and exhaustion, and asks a single question: "Did you read it? The last passage, in the corridor. Did you read it?" If the party says yes and can demonstrate comprehension — summarizing his argument, identifying his conclusion about the Dream, or simply acknowledging the work — Margolan nods once and gestures toward the orb. "Then someone knows. That is enough." He dissipates. Not dramatically, not with the controlled departure of Serenica's potential release — he simply loses coherence mid-gesture, his form thinning and scattering like smoke in a draft, and the labyrinth around the party begins to simplify. Walls recede. Passages straighten. The path back to the entrance becomes clear and direct, as though the structure that held the labyrinth together was Margolan himself, and without him the archive is returning to its original, orderly state.

If the party says no, or cannot answer — if they bypassed the final passage without reading, or read without understanding — Margolan's expression shifts to something between disappointment and resignation. He says nothing more. He dissipates in the same way, the labyrinth simplifies in the same way, and the orb is available for the taking. The difference is tonal rather than mechanical: a party that engaged with Margolan's work leaves the stronghold carrying knowledge that has value; a party that did not leaves carrying only the orb.

If the party attacks Margolan, he does not defend himself. He has neither the capability nor the interest. His form takes 1 point of damage from any source and dissipates immediately, the labyrinth collapsing in the same manner. The orb remains. The GM should not comment on this mechanically — the encounter is designed so that violence is technically possible and narratively empty. A party that destroys Margolan by force has gained nothing they would not have gained by speaking a single sentence, and has lost the opportunity to engage with the only mind on Nocturne capable of understanding its own destruction.

*GM note: The labyrinth encounter should reward engagement over brute force, but it should not punish parties that lack specific knowledge skills. The DCs are moderate for a level 16 mythic party, and the labyrinth is navigable even with failures — incorrect answers and failed checks extend the path and trigger hazards, but they do not create dead ends. A party with strong Knowledge skills will move through the labyrinth quickly and emerge with Margolan's analysis of the Dream. A party without those skills will take longer, face more hazards, and may miss the treatise in the final passage, but they will reach the orb. The spirit itself is not a combat threat, and parties that attempt to fight their way through the labyrinth will find that the architecture does not respond to violence — walls cannot be broken, passages cannot be forced, and area-effect spells targeted at the structure deal no damage and trigger additional defensive mechanisms (the labyrinth rearranges to extend the path by one additional chamber per spell used against its structure). The message should be clear without being stated: this is a place that rewards thinking.*

**Restoring the Second Bridge**

The second pylon stands at the far edge of Lexara's valley, identical in construction to the first — dark stone, carved channels, an empty socket at its crown. The orb seats itself with the same resonant tone, the channels ignite with the same branching light, and the bridge blazes to life across the second chasm with a harmonic that Lexara's enclosed architecture catches differently than Sonoria's open amphitheaters: the sound reverberates between the city's tall buildings, bouncing from wall to wall, filling the covered walkways and the reading rooms and the debate chambers with a sustained tone that hangs in the air like a word someone has spoken and no one has answered.

The Fetchlings of Lexara react as Sonoria's did — a pause, a turning of heads, a moment of attention directed at something genuinely new. But Lexara's reaction carries a different quality. In Sonoria, the Fetchlings paused in their music and stared. In Lexara, the debaters in the courtyard stop mid-argument and look at one another with expressions that are not quite confusion and not quite recognition — as though the sound of the bridge has reminded them of something they cannot name, a question they were about to ask that has slipped away before the words could form. The moment passes. The debates resume. But the chief archivist, Caelan, stands at the library's entrance for a long time after the sound fades, staring at the light of the bridge across the chasm with his intake forms held loosely in one hand, and for the first time in five centuries the forms do not look quite so absurd in his grip.

The third valley is visible beyond the bridge — broader than Lexara's, its walls carved in ways that suggest a different relationship with stone, the shapes of its architecture heavier and more imposing. The Valley of Sculpture. The chapter's set-piece battle waits on the other side.

---

### Scene 5: The Valley of Sculpture and Stronghold 3 — The Warlord's Redoubt

The third valley is the largest the party has entered — a broad, deep basin whose walls rise in sheer faces of pale stone that catch Nocturne's ambient light and throw it back in shades of grey and cream, the stone here lighter than the dark rock that characterizes the rest of the world. The reason is immediately apparent: the valley's stone is not a building material. It is a medium. The cliff faces have been carved. Not in the modest, functional manner of Sonoria's acoustic terracing or Lexara's archive entrances but on a monumental scale — entire mountainsides worked into bas-reliefs that depict scenes from Nocturne's history, its mythology, its artistic imagination. Figures thirty feet tall stride across vertical surfaces in processions that span hundreds of yards. Battles, festivals, coronations, and scenes of daily life rendered in stone with a naturalism that suggests sculptors who understood anatomy the way musicians understand harmony: as a system of relationships to be mastered and then transcended. The carvings are extraordinary. They are also, the party realizes with growing familiarity, the only sculptures in the valley. Everything on display was completed before the Dream fell. Nothing has been added since.

The city at the valley's center — **Lithara** — is built from the same pale stone as the cliffs, and its architecture has a weight and solidity that the previous two cities lacked. Where Sonoria was elegant and Lexara was dense, Lithara is monumental. The buildings are broad-shouldered, thick-walled, built to last in a way that suggests their architects thought in centuries. Public spaces are dominated by sculpture: freestanding figures in intersections, relief panels on building facades, carved friezes running along the upper stories of every major structure. The sculptures are uniformly excellent and uniformly old. The quarries that supplied the stone are visible at the valley's upper reaches — vast excavations cut into the mountainside, their floors littered with blocks of pale stone in various stages of extraction. The extraction stopped five centuries ago. The blocks remain where they were cut, some still partially attached to the bedrock, monuments to an interruption that the workers did not notice happening.

> *The valley opens around you in pale stone and arrested motion. The cliff faces are alive with figures — or they were once, when the hands that carved them understood what life looked like. Processions march across vertical surfaces in stone that holds the twilight's grey-violet light and softens it, the figures rendered with a precision that makes the mountain itself feel inhabited. The city below is built from the same stone, and the same impulse governs its construction: every surface that could carry a sculpture does, every building that could support a carved facade has been given one, and the overall effect is of a place where the boundary between architecture and art was considered artificial and abandoned. The quarries above the city are silent. The cranes that lifted the stone are still in position, their cables taut against loads that were being raised when time stopped. The workshops that line the city's main avenue have their doors open, their tools arranged on benches, their works in various states of completion — and every work in progress has been in the same state of progress for as long as anyone here can remember, which is not, as you have learned, very long at all.*

**The Dream's Third Face**

Lithara's Dream-bound population maintains the valley's sculptures with the same devoted precision the party has observed in previous valleys — polishing surfaces, repairing weather damage, replacing corroded fixings with identical replacements fabricated to original specifications. The maintenance is expert. The sculptors who perform it can discuss proportion, material properties, tool technique, and the history of every piece in the valley with the knowledge of master craftspeople. They cannot make anything new. The distinction between maintenance and creation is, in Lithara, more visible than anywhere else on Nocturne: the physical act of working stone is the same whether one is repairing an existing sculpture or carving a new one, and the Fetchlings of Lithara perform the first with consummate skill while being utterly incapable of the second. A sculptor working on a damaged figure can reshape a broken hand with confident, practiced strokes — but if asked to carve a figure of her own design, she reaches for her tools, considers the stone, and finds that she has nothing to say to it. She is not distressed by this. She returns to her maintenance work and does not mention the incident again.

The quarries are the most striking evidence. Lithara's sculptors were famous for working at monumental scale, and the quarries that supplied their stone were among Nocturne's largest industrial operations — hundreds of workers extracting, shaping, and transporting blocks that could weigh dozens of tons. The operation froze mid-process when the Dream fell. Blocks sit on transport sledges that have not moved. Cranes hold loads in positions that defy five centuries of weather and gravity, sustained by the same magitek systems that power the light bridges and the hydroponic farms — systems that continue to function at a fraction of their former capacity, enough to maintain stasis but not enough to support new work. A party member with Knowledge (Engineering) DC 12 recognizes that the quarry operation was in the middle of extracting a block of unusual size — easily forty feet on a side — and that the extraction was proceeding with a precision that suggests the block was intended for something specific. What that something was, no one in Lithara can say. The plans, if they existed, were in the mind of a sculptor who has died and reconstituted enough times that the plans are gone.

*GM note: The Valley of Sculpture shifts the Dream's tragedy from the invisible (Lexara's frozen intellectual life) to the monumental and physical. The evidence of what Lithara once was — and what it can no longer do — is literally carved into the landscape. The cliff-face bas-reliefs, the quarry cranes frozen in mid-lift, the workshops with unfinished works that will never be completed: these are the Dream's effects rendered at a scale that cannot be ignored or rationalized away. The party should feel, by the time they reach the stronghold, that they have seen three variations of the same catastrophe, each illuminating a different dimension of loss. Music was personal. Literature was institutional. Sculpture is civilizational — a culture's physical record, its most durable form of expression, stopped dead.*

**Stronghold 3 — The Warlord's Redoubt**

The third stronghold is not hidden in the valley wall or built into existing architecture. It dominates the valley's head — a fortress carved directly from the mountainside, its walls following the natural contours of the stone in a way that makes it difficult to tell where the mountain ends and the fortification begins. The design is militaristic in a way that no other structure on Nocturne has been: thick walls, narrow embrasures, overlapping fields of fire from elevated positions, a single approach path that winds up the mountainside in exposed switchbacks designed to keep attackers under observation for the entire ascent. This was not a concert hall or an archive repurposed by a spirit. This was built as a fortress by someone who understood war and expected it.

The spirit of the third stronghold is **Korvellan**, and he was everything the first two spirits were not. Where Serenica was an artist and Margolan was a scholar, Korvellan was a soldier — a Fetchling warlord who joined the Cabal not for artistic transcendence or intellectual access but for power, direct and undisguised. He was the Cabal's enforcer, the one who ensured that the sorcerers' more esoteric pursuits were protected by martial strength, and the Asura corruption that reached him did not need to work through a defining passion or an intellectual weakness. Korvellan wanted to be stronger, and the Asuras made him stronger, and the price was paid by everyone except Korvellan until Baselia hunted him down and killed him. Death has not changed his fundamental character. He is aggressive, territorial, and direct. He has spent five centuries fortifying his stronghold, building and commanding an army of construct guardians animated by the same spectral energy that sustains him, and waiting for someone to come and give him a reason to use them.

The party's approach does not go unnoticed. The stronghold's defenses activate when the party enters the final switchback — the first indication that this encounter will play differently from the previous two. Construct guardians emerge from alcoves cut into the approach path: humanoid figures of carved pale stone, their proportions exaggerated for combat — broader at the shoulder, thicker at the limb, their hands shaped into blunt instruments rather than fingers. They are animated sculptures in the most literal sense: figures pulled from the workshops and quarries of the valley below and repurposed for war, their original artistry still visible beneath the crude modifications Korvellan's spectral power has imposed on them. They move with a mechanical precision that lacks the fluid grace of living warriors but compensates with relentless, grinding efficiency. They do not speak. They do not hesitate. They advance in formation.

> *The fortress comes alive as you reach the final turn. Stone grinds on stone — a sound you feel in your teeth before you hear it in your ears — and figures emerge from the walls of the approach path. They were sculptures once. You can see it in the quality of the carving, the naturalistic proportions that someone has modified with brutal efficiency: shoulders broadened, limbs thickened, hands reshaped into hammers and blades of the same pale stone that forms their bodies. They step from their alcoves in unison, twelve of them forming a line across the path, and behind them the fortress gates grind open to reveal more — ranks of them, standing in the courtyard beyond, their blank faces oriented toward you with the patient attention of weapons waiting to be aimed.*
>
> *A voice reaches you from somewhere above — inside the fortress, resonating through the stone the way Serenica's music resonated through her concert hall, but where her voice carried grief, this one carries something simpler and more dangerous.*
>
> *"Finally."*

**The Battle**

This is the chapter's set-piece combat encounter — the largest and most complex fight the party faces on Nocturne, designed to test their tactical capabilities at the level 16 mythic tier 7 power threshold before they receive their level 17 advancement. The encounter is structured in three phases across the stronghold's vertical terrain, with Korvellan commanding his construct forces from the inner sanctum while engaging the party directly in the final phase.

**Phase 1: The Approach and Outer Courtyard.** The party must fight through the construct guardians on the approach path and into the outer courtyard. The constructs are individually moderate threats (use the Stone Golem base with reduced CR — treat as CR 11 each, with hardness 8, immunity to magic as per golem rules) but deployed in numbers: twelve on the approach path, another eight in the courtyard, with two larger constructs (CR 13, use Stone Golem stats as written) flanking the inner gate. The terrain is vertical — the approach path winds up the mountainside with sheer drops on one side, and the courtyard is overlooked by elevated firing positions where construct archers (use animated object statistics, Large, ranged attack +12, 2d6+4 damage) rain stone projectiles from above. The party must manage multiple threats across elevation changes while advancing toward the inner gate.

The constructs do not pursue beyond the courtyard if the party retreats. Korvellan is territorial, not strategic — he defends his stronghold but does not project force beyond it. A party that withdraws to rest and return faces the same garrison at full strength; the constructs repair themselves between engagements, drawing on the same magitek systems that sustain the valley's infrastructure.

**Phase 2: The Interior — Workshops and Forges.** Beyond the inner gate, the stronghold's character changes. The original structure was a sculptor's complex — workshops, forges, material stores — and Korvellan has converted it to an armory. The workshops now produce construct bodies rather than sculptures, and the forges that once heated bronze for casting now heat stone through magitek processes that make it malleable enough to shape into war-forms. The interior is a series of connected chambers at different elevations, linked by ramps, bridges over forge-pits, and carved stairways — a three-dimensional battlespace that rewards mobility and punishes static tactics.

The interior is defended by Korvellan's elite constructs — four war-sculptures of significantly greater sophistication than the courtyard garrison. These are CR 14 constructs (use Advanced Stone Golem statistics with the following modifications: +2 to attack rolls, +10 hp, and a Mythic Smash ability that allows them to expend one use of mythic power to deal double damage on a single melee attack, usable 1/day each). They fight with coordinated tactics — flanking, using terrain to force the party into forge-pits (4d6 fire damage per round of contact with the heated stone), collapsing bridges to split the party across elevation gaps (Reflex DC 18 to avoid falling, 3d6 falling damage plus prone).
