Korvellan's voice echoes through the interior throughout this phase, directing his constructs with clipped commands that suggest a professional military mind — he is not taunting the party but managing a battle with the focused attention of a commander who takes his work seriously.

**Phase 3: The Inner Sanctum.** The deepest chamber of the stronghold is a natural cavern that Korvellan has expanded into a throne room of sorts — a high-ceilinged space with a raised dais at one end, the orb mounted in a cradle of dark iron behind it, and Korvellan himself standing at the center of the space in full manifestation. Unlike Serenica's flickering form or Margolan's dissolving coherence, Korvellan's spirit has achieved a density that borders on physical presence. He is a massive figure — a Fetchling warrior rendered in spectral stone, his form solid enough to interact with the physical world, his weapons real enough to draw blood. He has spent five centuries feeding his martial essence into this form, sacrificing memory, personality, and everything that made him a person in exchange for combat capability. What remains is a warlord stripped to his fundamental function: the ability to fight, and the desire to do so.

Korvellan fights alone in Phase 3 — his remaining constructs hold the interior rather than reinforcing the sanctum, a tactical choice that reflects his personality. He does not want help. He wants a battle worth having. His full stat block is in the appendix (see Stat Block Appendix, Korvellan entry — CR 17), but the key tactical elements are: his Spectral Density ability grants him DR 15/adamantine and magic, making him extremely difficult to damage with conventional weapons; his Stone Commander ability allows him to animate sections of the cavern walls and floor as improvised constructs (treat as Medium animated objects, 2 per round as a free action, maximum 6 active at once); and his Forge Strike ability channels the magitek heat of the stronghold's forges through his melee attacks, adding 2d6 fire damage and forcing a Fort DC 20 save or the target's armor or shield is heated (as *heat metal*, beginning at the third round of effect). The sanctum's terrain includes forge vents in the floor that erupt on initiative count 10 each round (Reflex DC 16 to avoid, 4d6 fire damage, 10-foot radius), and Korvellan knows their positions and uses them to his advantage.

The fight should be the hardest the party has faced on Nocturne and should feel earned. Korvellan is not a tragic figure in the way Serenica and Margolan were — he chose violence freely, embraced the Cabal for power he used to harm others, and has spent his afterlife building an army. The party should not feel conflicted about destroying him. The complexity of the encounter is tactical, not moral.

> *The spirit stands in the center of the chamber as though he has been waiting — and he has, you realize, for five centuries, with the patience of a soldier who knows the battle will come eventually and has used every moment of the waiting to prepare for it. He is enormous. Not in the way of the Hishandura's grotesque bulk, but in the way of something that has been built for a purpose and built well — broad, dense, his spectral form carrying the solidity of the stone he has spent centuries shaping and commanding. He holds a hammer in one hand and a shield in the other, both carved from the same pale stone as the valley's sculptures, and his eyes — the only part of him that reads as something other than carved — burn with a cold light that is not rage and not madness but something more dangerous: competence.*
>
> *"Good," he says, and his voice does not echo in the chamber because the chamber was designed not to echo. "I was beginning to think no one would come."*

**The Magitek Horse Constructs**

After Korvellan is destroyed and the sanctum secured, the party discovers a sealed chamber behind the dais — a workshop of a different character than the armory above. The room is clean, orderly, and untouched by Korvellan's modifications. The magitek systems here are more sophisticated than anything else in the stronghold — not the brute forges that heated stone for war-constructs but precision instruments of a caliber that suggests a different maker entirely. Six stalls line the walls, each containing a dormant construct in the shape of a horse.

The constructs are beautiful in the way that fine engineering is beautiful — not naturalistic, not attempting to pass for living horses, but designed with an elegance that speaks of a maker who understood both function and aesthetics. Their bodies are articulated plates of dark metal — not iron or steel but something with the sheen and weight of bronze and the hardness of adamantine, a Vatrasi alloy that the party may recognize if they encountered Kerlin Whitemane's other works on Vatra. Their joints are smooth, their proportions precise, their heads shaped with just enough suggestion of equine anatomy to read as horses without descending into mimicry. Each construct is roughly the size of a heavy warhorse, and their stalls contain charging cradles connected to the stronghold's magitek power grid — the constructs have been drawing a trickle of maintenance power for five centuries, keeping their systems intact even in dormancy.

When the party enters the workshop, the constructs respond. Not to voice or touch but to something subtler: the mythic power that the party carries, the same divine-adjacent energy that the constructs were built to serve. Their activation is not dramatic — no grinding gears, no shower of sparks. One by one, in sequence, their eyes open. The eyes are lenses of amber crystal that glow with a warm internal light, and when they focus on the party the quality of attention behind them is unmistakable. These are not automatons. They are intelligent — aware, evaluative, making decisions about the beings who have entered their stable with the quiet deliberation of animals assessing whether a stranger is a threat or a friend. The first construct to move does so with a fluid grace that the stone guardians above could not approach: it steps from its stall, lowers its head, and studies the nearest party member with an expression that is difficult to describe as anything other than curious.

> *The first construct steps forward and you understand immediately that this is something different from the stone things you fought in the corridors above. It moves like water over stone — every joint articulated, every motion purposeful, the dark metal of its body catching the workshop's dim light and holding it the way a horse's coat holds sunlight. It lowers its head and looks at you. The amber eyes are warm and sharp and undeniably intelligent, and the attention they pay you is not the blank assessment of a golem checking its target list but something older and more personal. It is deciding whether it trusts you. The decision takes three heartbeats. Then it steps forward again, close enough to touch, and presses its metal forehead against your chest with a gentleness that has no business existing in something made of bronze and adamantine.*

The constructs were built by **Kerlin Whitemane** — the Warlock of Vatra, the artificer genius whose magitek creations define much of the Nine Worlds' infrastructure — and gifted to Baselia before the falling out that turned the ten heroes against one another. They were her personal mounts, built for her paladins, designed to respond to divine power and serve those who carried it. The corruption that made Baselia an anti-paladin did not destroy the constructs — it rendered them dormant, their systems recognizing that the power they were built to serve had been inverted and refusing to function under its new polarity. They have been waiting in this workshop for five centuries for someone carrying the right kind of power to walk through the door.

The constructs serve the party for the remainder of the campaign. Their full stat block is in the appendix (see Stat Block Appendix, Magitek Horse Construct entry), but the key characteristics are: they are intelligent (Int 10, Wis 14, Cha 8), loyal to the party once bonded, tireless (immune to fatigue and exhaustion, do not need to eat or sleep), fast (60 ft. land speed, 40 ft. climb speed on stone surfaces), and durable (hardness 10, hp 85, construct immunities). They do not speak but communicate through behavior — ear position, head movement, shifts in gait, and the intensity of the amber glow in their eyes. They understand Common and can follow complex verbal commands. Six constructs are available, enough for the full party with spares if the party numbers fewer than six.

One detail the party may notice: when the constructs leave the workshop and enter the stronghold's corridors, they orient toward the valley's far end — toward the direction of the Citadel of Lament, still two valleys and two bridges away. Their ears flatten. Their gait shortens. The amber glow in their eyes dims and takes on a troubled quality that does not resolve until the party moves them away from the line of sight. The constructs remember Baselia. They remember what she was. They can sense what she has become. The reaction is not dramatic — it is the quiet distress of creatures who loved their mistress and know that something has gone terribly wrong with her — but it is unmistakable, and it serves as the first emotional indicator from a non-verbal source about what awaits at the chapter's climax.

*GM note: The magitek horse constructs are a significant reward — mechanically powerful mounts that will serve the party through the campaign's remaining chapters — and should be presented as such. Their intelligence is genuine, not simulated: they make decisions, express preferences, and form relationships with their riders that develop over time. A party member who treats their construct well (grooming the metal plates, speaking to it, respecting its distress when facing the Citadel's direction) should find that the construct responds with increased responsiveness and initiative. The constructs' reaction to Baselia's direction is not a plot mechanic — the party cannot use it as a compass or a divination tool — but it is an emotional thread that the GM can pull on throughout the remainder of the chapter. The constructs loved Baselia. Whatever she has become, they remember what she was, and their grief for her is real even though they cannot express it in words.*

**Milestone: Level 17**

The party advances to level 17 after the Stronghold 3 battle. This represents the chapter's midpoint in both structure and difficulty — the party has cleared three of five strongholds, restored three of five bridges, and the challenges ahead (infiltration, moral choice, and the Citadel itself) will test the new capabilities that level 17 provides. The advancement should be presented as earned: the set-piece battle was the hardest fight on Nocturne so far, Korvellan was the most dangerous opponent since the Hishandura, and the party has demonstrated the tactical capability required to face what remains.

**Restoring the Third Bridge**

The third bridge blazes to life with the same mechanics as the first two but a different quality — the harmonic that the valley's pale stone produces is deeper, more resonant, a bass note that vibrates through the carved cliff faces and sets the monumental bas-reliefs trembling in their stone. In Lithara, the effect is visible: fine stone dust shakes free from sculpture surfaces that have been perfectly maintained for five centuries, and for a moment the figures carved into the mountainside seem to shift, their poses adjusting by fractions of an inch as the vibration passes through them. The Fetchling sculptors in the quarry pause in their maintenance work and look up at the cliff faces with expressions the party has learned to recognize — that flicker of almost-awareness, the Dream cracking at its edges before resealing itself around the minds it holds.

The fourth valley is visible beyond the bridge. Its walls are covered in color — the first color the party has seen on Nocturne that is not a shade of grey, violet, or the pale cream of Lithara's stone. Murals. Frescoes. Paintings on every surface, their pigments still vivid after five centuries in the twilight, covering the canyon walls in images that the party cannot yet resolve from this distance but that seem, in the shifting quality of Nocturne's light, to move.

---

### Scene 6: The Valley of Painting and Stronghold 4 — The Palace of Veils

The fourth valley is, for the first time since arriving on Nocturne, beautiful in a way that does not require qualification. The previous three valleys were striking — Sonoria's acoustic architecture, Lexara's dense intellectualism, Lithara's monumental carving — but their beauty was formal, structural, expressed in the arrangement of stone and space. The Valley of Painting is beautiful in color, and color is something this world has been starving the party of since they stepped through the terminus arch. The canyon walls are covered in murals. Not decorated — covered, every exposed surface from the valley floor to the highest reachable point painted in pigments that have survived five centuries of twilight with their vibrancy intact, preserved by the same ambient magitek energy that sustains the infrastructure and the Dream-bound population. The subjects range from the representational to the abstract, from intimate portraiture to landscapes that span entire cliff faces, and the quality is uniformly extraordinary — these were not the casual decorations of amateurs but the deliberate, sustained output of a culture that considered the painting of public surfaces a civic duty on par with the building of roads.

The city in the valley's center — **Chromara** — is the most visually overwhelming settlement the party has visited on Nocturne. Every building is a canvas. Facades are painted in elaborate compositions that interact with the architecture they cover — a mural of a forest on a building's front wall extends around the corners to become a garden on the sides, with painted birds that seem to fly from one surface to the next as the viewer walks around the structure. Interior walls continue the exterior themes. Streets are laid out so that the murals on facing buildings create continuous scenes across the gap, the perspective calculated to resolve into a single image when viewed from specific points marked by small stone circles set into the pavement. The Fetchlings of Chromara were not merely painters — they were environmental artists who treated the city itself as a single, integrated composition, and the result is a place where walking down a street feels like moving through the interior of a painting that has been folded into three dimensions.

> *Color. After three valleys of grey stone and violet twilight, the fourth valley strikes you like a physical thing. The canyon walls are alive with it — not the metaphorical life of Lithara's carved figures but the vivid, breathing presence of pigment and light, thousands of paintings covering every surface the eye can reach. You see landscapes that stretch across cliff faces as though the mountain has become a window into another place. You see portraits ten feet tall, their subjects gazing out from the rock with expressions so specific that they must have been painted from life. You see abstractions — vast fields of color that have no subject but their own arrangement, patterns that shift and pulse in Nocturne's twilight as the angle of the light changes, the paintings responding to the world's perpetual not-quite-dawn in ways their creators must have anticipated and designed for.*
>
> *The city below continues the effect. Every building is painted, every surface used, every wall a composition that interacts with the walls around it in ways that make the distinction between architecture and art not merely blurred but irrelevant. The Fetchlings who move through these streets walk through a world that was designed to be looked at, and they do look — they pause at corners, they study familiar paintings with the appreciation of people who notice things they have not noticed before. Except they have noticed them before. Every time. For five hundred years.*

**The Dream's Fourth Face**

The Valley of Painting presents the Dream's cruelest paradox. In Sonoria, the Fetchlings could not create new music but they could still perform existing works with feeling. In Lexara, they could not generate new ideas but they could still engage with old ones. In Lithara, they could not carve new sculptures but they could still maintain old ones with expert skill. In Chromara, the Dream's prohibition on creation is at its most visible and its most strange, because the medium itself is so immediate. A musician's failure to compose is invisible — silence leaves no evidence. A sculptor's failure to carve leaves a blank stone that might simply be a stone. But an empty wall in a city where every wall is painted is a wound that everyone can see and no one can explain.

The Dream-bound painters of Chromara spend their days maintaining the existing murals — retouching faded pigments, repairing weather damage to exposed surfaces, mixing paints from recipes they learned before the curse — and they do this work with the same consummate skill the party has observed in every other valley. The maintenance is indistinguishable from original work: the retouching is so precise that a restored section cannot be differentiated from the surrounding paint even under close examination. The painters are brilliant technicians. They can match any color, replicate any brushstroke, reproduce any effect that the original artists achieved. They simply cannot use those skills to produce anything that was not already there.

The evidence accumulates. A painter standing before a blank section of wall — a surface exposed by a minor rockfall that removed the painted face above it — holds her brush with confidence, considers the bare stone, and cannot begin. She stands there for hours. Other Fetchlings pass her without comment. Eventually she returns to retouching a mural on the adjacent wall, and if asked about the blank section she gestures at it with mild puzzlement and says, "Someone will get to it." No one will. The blank sections are scattered throughout the valley — not many, perhaps a dozen in the entire city, where minor damage has exposed unpainted stone — and they stand out against the surrounding color with the starkness of missing teeth. The painters see them. They intend to fill them. The intention has been the same for five centuries.

A gallery carved into the mountainside contains pre-curse works displayed on movable panels — the closest thing Chromara has to a museum, a curated collection of individual works presented outside their architectural context. The gallery is well-attended and the Fetchlings who visit discuss the works with genuine insight: composition, color theory, the relationship between a painter's intent and the viewer's perception. A party member with Craft (Art) or another relevant skill who engages in these conversations finds them sophisticated and rewarding — the Dream-bound painters have not lost their critical faculty, only their generative one. They can recognize brilliance. They can analyze technique. They can articulate what makes a painting succeed or fail with a precision that would be enviable in any art school. They cannot pick up a brush and demonstrate what they mean.

*GM note: Chromara should feel different from the previous valleys not only in the specifics of its art form but in its emotional register. The previous three valleys presented the Dream's tragedy through absence — the silence of unwritten music, the stasis of frozen arguments, the stillness of uncarved stone. Chromara presents it through presence: the color is there, the skill is there, the critical understanding is there, and the blank walls are there too, visible reminders of what is missing in a medium that makes absence impossible to ignore. The paintings themselves should be described with genuine appreciation — the GM is not merely setting a scene but presenting the output of a civilization that considered visual art its highest expression. The beauty is real. The grief is that the beauty cannot grow.*

**Stronghold 4 — The Palace of Veils**

The fourth stronghold occupies a structure at the valley's far edge that appears, from the outside, to be the grandest building in Chromara — a palace of dark stone whose facade is painted in murals of such scale and accomplishment that the party may mistake it for a civic building or a temple. The entrance is open. The interior is lit. The painted corridors that lead inward are beautiful and welcoming and present no obvious threat. This is deliberate. The fourth spirit is not a warrior like Korvellan or a recluse like Margolan. She is a manipulator, and her stronghold is designed to be entered, not assaulted.

The spirit of the fourth stronghold is **Verithan**, and she was, in life, the most dangerous of the five Cabal sorcerers — not in terms of raw power but in terms of what she chose to do with it. She was a painter of extraordinary talent who turned to the Cabal not for creative transcendence but for control. Her art had always been about the relationship between perception and reality — works that challenged the viewer's assumptions, that used technique to make the impossible appear true and the true appear impossible — and the Asura-corrupted power of the Cabal gave her the tools to extend that principle beyond canvas and into the world itself. In life, she was an illusionist of staggering capability. In death, she has become something worse: a spirit whose command of illusion is so complete that the boundary between what she creates and what exists has, within the walls of her stronghold, been effectively dissolved.

Unlike the previous spirits, Verithan has not withdrawn from the Dream-bound population. She has engaged with it. Over the centuries she has taken Fetchlings from the valley — quietly, one or two at a time, never enough to create a gap that the Dream-bound would notice — and brought them into her stronghold. Some serve as attendants, maintaining the palace's interior under conditions they do not recognize as imprisonment. Some have become subjects for her art: she paints them, not on canvas but through illusion, altering their perception of themselves and their surroundings until they inhabit realities that exist only within the palace's walls. Some have been killed and reconstituted inside the stronghold so many times that they have no memory of the valley outside — they believe they have always lived in the palace, that its painted corridors are the entirety of the world, and that Verithan is not their captor but their patron.

The palace's interior is a labyrinth of a different kind than Margolan's. Where his was built on intellectual logic, Verithan's is built on perceptual deception. Corridors that appear to lead forward actually curve back on themselves. Rooms whose doors open onto one space at one moment open onto another space the next. Painted surfaces become three-dimensional passages; three-dimensional passages flatten into painted surfaces. The effect is not random — it is controlled, deliberate, the work of an artist who understands perspective, light, shadow, and the assumptions that the brain makes when processing visual information, and who has spent five centuries turning that understanding into a weapon. *True seeing* cuts through the illusions but reveals the stronghold's true architecture in a way that is disorienting in its own right: the actual layout is a tight, cramped series of cells and corridors that bear no relationship to the expansive, beautiful spaces the illusions project over them.

> *The palace opens around you in painted splendor. The entrance corridor is wide and high-ceilinged, its walls covered in murals that depict scenes of celebration — figures dancing, musicians playing, tables laid with food and drink — rendered with a realism so precise that you can almost hear the music. The corridor leads to a gallery whose proportions are generous and whose displays are magnificent: paintings on every wall, arranged with the eye of a curator who understands how works interact with each other and with the space that contains them. Light comes from somewhere above — warm, steady, the first artificial light you have encountered on Nocturne that does not carry the cold luminescence of magitek but instead suggests something almost like sunlight.*
>
> *It is perfect. Every surface, every angle, every source of light has been considered and controlled with an attention to detail that goes beyond expertise and into obsession. The beauty is deliberate and complete and designed to make you feel welcome.*
>
> *That is the first thing that should make you suspicious.*

**The Challenge**

The stronghold is an infiltration and rescue encounter. The party must locate the captive Fetchlings, free them from the palace, and reclaim the orb — and they must do so within an environment where their senses are actively unreliable. The GM should structure this as a series of challenges that reward stealth, perception, and precision over brute force.

**The Illusory Architecture.** The palace's layout changes based on Verithan's will. Corridors loop. Rooms relocate. Exits appear and vanish. The party cannot map the stronghold through conventional means — any map drawn while inside the palace is inaccurate within minutes as the illusions shift around them. *True seeing* reveals the actual architecture but imposes a different problem: the real layout is a claustrophobic network of cells, and a character using *true seeing* must reconcile what they see with what their companions see, leading to situations where one party member is trying to navigate a narrow corridor while the rest believe they are in a grand hall. Perception DC 20 (or DC 14 with *true seeing*) allows a character to identify the seams between illusion and reality — points where painted walls meet actual walls, where the light behaves differently, where the architecture's geometry violates physical law in ways that an attentive observer can detect. Each successful check reveals a stable landmark that the party can use for navigation — a fixed point in a shifting space.

**The Captive Fetchlings.** Verithan's prisoners are distributed throughout the palace in three groups. The first group — approximately a dozen Fetchlings — serves as the palace's visible population, attending to maintenance tasks in the illusory grand corridors. They are Dream-bound and do not know they are captives. They believe the palace is their home and Verithan is their beloved patron. They are not hostile to the party but will resist any attempt to remove them from the palace, not through violence but through confused insistence that there is nothing wrong and nowhere else they would rather be. Persuading them to leave requires either breaking Verithan's local illusion (dispelling the glamour on a specific Fetchling, Dispel Magic CL 17) or physically carrying them past the palace's threshold, at which point the illusory overlay drops and the Fetchling experiences a disorienting moment of clarity before the Dream reasserts itself. They do not thank the party. They do not understand what has happened. They simply find themselves outside a building they do not remember entering and wander back toward the valley with the mild confusion of someone who has lost their train of thought.

The second group — perhaps six Fetchlings — is imprisoned in the palace's hidden cells, the real architecture beneath the illusions. These Fetchlings have been killed and reconstituted inside the stronghold enough times that they have no memory of the valley at all. They are passive, compliant, and utterly lost. Finding them requires navigating the true layout — which means either sustained use of *true seeing* or successful Perception checks to locate the hidden cell doors. The cells are not locked. Verithan does not need locks. The prisoners do not know there is an outside.

The third group is a complication: three Fetchlings who have been altered by Verithan's art so extensively that they cannot perceive reality even outside the palace. They see painted visions overlaid on the world at all times — beautiful, compelling visions that Verithan crafted specifically for each of them, personalized illusions that provide each Fetchling with a reality more appealing than the one they actually inhabit. Removing them from the palace does not end the effect. Only a *break enchantment* (CL 17), *dispel magic* at CL 20, or *heal* will strip the persistent illusions. Without intervention, these three Fetchlings will wander through the valley seeing a world that does not exist, interacting with people who are not there, and presenting a visible, unsettling manifestation of what Verithan's power can do to a mind.

**Verithan Herself.** The spirit does not engage the party directly unless forced. She observes them through the palace's illusions — every painted surface is a window for her, every wall a vantage point — and she responds to their presence by manipulating the environment. Corridors shift to separate party members. Illusions create false threats (monsters that cannot deal damage but provoke reactions) and false allies (Fetchlings who appear to need help but lead the party deeper into the palace's disorienting architecture). If the party advances toward the orb without engaging with the rescue, Verithan allows it — the orb is kept in the palace's deepest chamber, behind layers of illusion but not behind any physical barrier. She does not consider the orb important. She considers the Fetchlings important. They are her art collection, and her art collection is the only thing she has that matters.

If the party reaches the orb chamber without rescuing the Fetchlings, Verithan manifests — a translucent figure whose form shifts between her living appearance (a Fetchling woman of severe beauty, her features precise, her expression controlled) and a version of herself painted in visible brushstrokes, as though she is simultaneously a person and a portrait of a person. She does not fight. She speaks. Her voice carries the same controlled composure she brought to everything in life and death, and what she says is designed to make the party question whether they should take the orb at all. The captive Fetchlings are happy, she points out. Happier than the Dream-bound population in the valley, who maintain their hollow routines without even the comfort of beautiful illusions. She has given her captives something the Dream took from the rest: a world worth looking at. The fact that the world is not real is, she argues, irrelevant — the Dream-bound population's reality is not real either, but at least her version is beautiful.

If the party takes the orb and leaves without rescuing anyone, Verithan does not resist. She has no interest in a fight she might lose over an object she does not value. The orb is taken, the bridge can be restored, and the captive Fetchlings remain in the palace. This is a valid outcome. It is not the right one, and the GM should ensure the party understands that the Fetchlings are still inside — not through Verithan's words, which are self-serving, but through the visible evidence: the attendants in the corridors who smiled and welcomed them, the hidden cells they may have discovered, the three Fetchlings whose perception has been permanently altered. The party can choose to leave them. They should know what they are choosing.

If the party attacks Verithan, she fights — but she fights the way an illusionist fights, which is to say she does not. The party fights her illusions. Verithan's actual form is incorporeal and fragile (hp 60, no meaningful combat abilities), but she can project up to three illusory duplicates of herself that appear solid, deal apparent damage (Will DC 22 to disbelieve; failed saves result in nonlethal damage that feels real), and occupy the party while she repositions through the palace's walls. The fight is not about overpowering the party — it is about exhausting them, disorienting them, and buying time for her to relocate her captives to deeper cells. A party with strong Will saves and access to *true seeing* can end the fight quickly by locating and destroying her actual form. A party without those tools may spend considerable time fighting phantoms while Verithan watches from behind a painted wall.

A frontal assault is possible but costly — not in damage but in consequences. The more chaos the party creates inside the palace, the more disoriented the captive Fetchlings become. Spells that deal area damage may strike captives hidden behind illusory walls. Dispelling magic targeted at the palace's illusions en masse causes the entire population of the stronghold — captives and all — to experience the sudden, traumatic collapse of the only reality they know. The GM should not prevent the party from fighting through the palace, but the infiltration approach is rewarded: a party that moves quietly, identifies the real architecture, locates the captives, and extracts them before confronting Verithan accomplishes the rescue cleanly. A party that kicks in the front door and starts casting may save everyone, or may cause harm they did not intend.

*GM note: Stronghold 4 is designed to test a different set of capabilities than the previous three encounters. Stronghold 1 rewarded diplomacy. Stronghold 2 rewarded knowledge. Stronghold 3 rewarded combat prowess. Stronghold 4 rewards perception, restraint, and the willingness to prioritize people over objectives. A party that goes straight for the orb can get it easily — Verithan does not guard it — but the rescue is the real challenge, and the party's choices about who to save, how much time to spend, and whether to engage Verithan at all determine the scene's emotional outcome. The captive Fetchlings are Dream-bound and cannot fully understand what has been done to them; freeing them is not a triumphant rescue but a complicated act of uncertain mercy that echoes the chapter's central question about whether awareness of suffering is better than oblivion.*

**Restoring the Fourth Bridge**

The fourth orb seats itself in the pylon at the valley's edge, and the bridge blazes to life in color. Not the warm golden light of the previous bridges but a prismatic display — the orb's energy refracting through Chromara's painted canyon walls, the bridge's illumination picking up pigment from the surrounding murals and casting it outward in bands of color that sweep across the chasm like the arc of a painter's brush. The harmonic that the valley produces is higher than Lithara's deep bass, a clear tone that rings through the painted streets and sets the murals vibrating at a frequency that makes the figures in them seem, for one breathless moment, to move. Not the illusion of movement that the twilight's shifting quality produces — actual movement, painted figures turning their heads, painted eyes focusing on the light of the bridge, painted hands reaching toward it. The moment passes. The paintings are still. But the Fetchling painters in Chromara have stopped what they are doing — every one of them, across the entire valley, simultaneously — and they are staring at the murals with an expression the party has not seen on a Dream-bound face before. Not the flicker of almost-awareness. Not the momentary pause. Something deeper. Something that looks, for the space of a held breath, like grief.

The moment breaks. The painters return to their work. But the painter standing before the blank wall — the one who has been holding her brush for five centuries without making a mark — has not moved. She is still staring at the wall. Her brush is still raised. And her hand, for the first time in five hundred years, is shaking.

Beyond the bridge, the valley widens into a junction where two cities face each other across a chasm. The fifth and final bridge — the one that leads to the Citadel of Lament — is broken between them. The Twin Cities. The chapter's quiet moment before the storm.

---

### Scene 7: The Twin Cities

The junction between Valleys 4 and 5 is the widest open space the party has encountered on Nocturne — a broad shelf of rock where the mountain ranges that define the individual valleys pull back, creating a natural amphitheater several miles across. Two cities occupy this space, built on facing cliffs above a chasm that drops into the same absolute darkness the party has seen beneath every broken bridge. The cities mirror each other in scale and general architecture — dark stone, elegant lines, the Fetchling aesthetic the party has come to recognize — but their character diverges in ways that become apparent as the party approaches. The city on the near side, which the party reaches first, is built for display: its buildings feature broad facades, open fronts, stages and platforms visible from the streets, and a central district dominated by a structure the party can identify even from a distance as a theater — a vast open-air performance space carved into the cliff face, its tiered seating oriented to face the chasm and the far city beyond it. The city on the far side, visible across the gap, is built for work: denser, more industrial, its buildings closed-fronted and utilitarian, its streets narrower, its skyline punctuated by the shapes of workshops and warehouses rather than stages and galleries.

The two cities were once a single metropolis — **Dramara** — the cultural capital of Nocturne's fifth and most collaborative art form: theater. The near city was the performance half: the stages, the auditoriums, the rehearsal spaces, the academies where actors trained and directors planned and playwrights debated. The far city was the production half: the workshops where sets were built, costumes sewn, instruments made, stage machinery engineered, and the thousand material requirements of theatrical performance manufactured by craftspeople who considered their work as essential to the art as the performers'. The light bridge that once connected them was not merely a transit route but the central artery of a creative ecosystem — performers crossed to consult with set designers; costumers crossed to fit actors; directors crossed daily, moving between rehearsal and construction with the fluidity that the art required. The bridge's destruction severed the ecosystem in half, and the Dream sealed the wound shut. The two halves of Dramara have continued their routines in isolation for five centuries, each performing its function without the other, neither side capable of noticing that the collaboration that defined their art has ended.

> *Two cities face each other across darkness. They are close enough to see clearly — close enough to shout across — and the architecture on each side speaks of a relationship that was once intimate and is now severed. The near city is built for an audience: stages open to the chasm, seating oriented toward the far side, the entire urban plan designed to face outward, toward a partner it can no longer reach. The far city is built for labor: workshops and warehouses, the infrastructure of making things, its streets oriented inward, toward work that has no destination. Between them the chasm drops into blackness, and the pylons of the bridge that once connected them rise from the cliff edges like the stumps of severed fingers, reaching toward each other across a gap they cannot close.*
>
> *The theater at the near city's center is the largest performance space you have seen on Nocturne. Its stage faces the chasm. Its seating rises in tiers that could hold thousands. It was built so that an audience could watch a performance while looking past the stage toward the far city, toward the workshops where the performance was made — a deliberate architectural statement that the art and the labor that produced it were part of the same experience. Now the stage faces nothing. The far city's lights glow across the gap, unreachable, and the theater runs its season to an audience that watches plays performed on a stage designed for a view that no longer exists.*

**The Dream at Scale**

The Twin Cities are the largest population center the party has visited on Nocturne, and the Dream's effects at this scale produce something the party has not experienced in the individual valleys: the weight of sheer numbers. Hundreds of Fetchlings, going about the motions of cultural life across two cities, maintaining routines that lost their purpose five centuries ago. The cumulative effect is not horror — the party has had four valleys to adjust to the Dream's specific cruelty — but exhaustion, the particular weariness that comes from witnessing a catastrophe so vast and so normalized that the mind begins to accept it as simply the way things are. The GM should lean into this. The Twin Cities are the point in the chapter where the party risks becoming acclimated to the Dream the same way the Fetchlings have, and the GM's job is to make the party feel that pull — the temptation to stop seeing the wrongness, to accept the pleasant surface, to treat the Dream-bound population as scenery rather than victims — and then to puncture it.

The near city's theater runs an opera season. The season consists of twelve works performed in rotation, the same twelve works it has performed since before the Dream fell. The productions are technically superb — the Fetchling performers are skilled, the direction is precise, the music (provided by a pit orchestra whose members are as Dream-bound as the actors) is accomplished. The operas tell stories of love, loss, betrayal, triumph, and transcendence — the full range of emotional experience, rendered with apparent feeling by performers who are incapable of genuine feeling because the Dream has replaced their inner life with a perfect, hollow replica. A party member who attends a performance sees the final paradox of Nocturne's curse: art that is about the experience of being alive, performed by people who are not alive, for an audience that cannot tell the difference, in a theater designed to showcase a connection to the production city that no longer exists. The performance is beautiful. It means nothing. The audience's applause is warm and sincere and will be identical tomorrow night and the night after and every night until someone from outside comes to change it.

The far city's workshops maintain their readiness with the same commitment the party has observed everywhere on Nocturne. Costumers keep fabric in stock, cut patterns, and maintain existing costumes with expert skill. Set builders maintain tools and workspaces and repair existing set pieces that no one has commissioned new ones to replace. A puppet-maker's workshop contains dozens of exquisite marionettes, each maintained to performance standard, none of them new. The workshops are prepared for commissions that will never come from a performance city that cannot reach them, and the far city's population finds this state of affairs entirely normal. They are ready. They have been ready for five hundred years. Readiness, in the absence of purpose, has become its own purpose.

The party can move freely between the two half-cities by crossing the chasm — flight, teleportation, or creative use of the terrain (the chasm is not infinitely wide; at its narrowest point, a rope bridge or similar improvisation could span it, though the depth beneath is real and the darkness absolute). The fifth stronghold is on the far side of the far city, at the entrance to Valley 5. But the party should spend time in the Twin Cities before moving on. This is the chapter's breath before the climax — the last space where the world's tragedy is on full display before the narrative narrows to the Citadel and Baselia — and the emotional weight of four restored bridges and four reclaimed valleys should be given room to settle.

**The Tamaron Recruitment Point**

If Tamaron was turned on Illium and the party intends to bring him to the Citadel, the Twin Cities are the natural staging point for that operation. The party has restored four bridges — four of the five connections between the valleys are live — and the fifth bridge, the one that leads to the Citadel, will be restored once Stronghold 5 is cleared. The logistics of recruiting Tamaron should feel real and deliberate, not trivial.

The party can contact Tamaron through *sending* (or similar long-range communication) while in the Twin Cities. Tamaron is on Illium, slowly rebuilding. His response to the request is immediate and unequivocal: he will come. He does not hesitate, does not bargain, does not ask for time. If the party tells him that Baselia needs him, he responds with the blunt simplicity of a man who has been waiting for this exact request without knowing it: "Tell me where. I am coming." The party must arrange his transport — either returning to Nexus via the Rainbow Road and escorting him to Nocturne, or directing him to the Nocturne gate town and meeting him at the first valley. The journey takes time: at minimum, a day of travel each way if the party uses the Rainbow Road directly, longer if complications arise. The party can send one or two members to escort Tamaron while the rest proceed to Stronghold 5, or they can go together and accept the time cost.

Tamaron arrives on Nocturne gaunt, quiet, and visibly affected by the world's twilight. He has spent five centuries possessed by an Asura lord, and the months since his liberation have not been enough to restore him fully. He walks with the careful economy of a man who has recently relearned the use of his own body. His divine power, severed for centuries, has begun to return but is not yet reliable — he can channel positive energy in short bursts, his healing is inconsistent, and his aura of good flickers rather than blazing. He is not the paladin he was. He is the man who is trying to become that paladin again, and the effort is visible in everything he does.

When Tamaron sees Nocturne — the twilight, the Dream-bound Fetchlings, the evidence of a world frozen in grief — his reaction is the one thing the Dream cannot produce: genuine anguish. He knows what happened here. He knows who did it. He knows that the woman who did it was driven to it in part by his own actions — his rejection of her, his retreat into solitude, his failure to see what his abandonment would cost until it had cost everything. He does not speak about this unprompted. If the party asks, he answers with the same directness the Old Man displayed: "I left her. She broke. Everything that followed was built on that breaking." He does not absolve himself. He does not ask the party to absolve him. He walks through the Twin Cities with the magitek horse constructs trailing behind him, and the constructs' reaction to his presence is notable — they recognize him. Not as a threat, not as a friend, but as someone connected to the person they are grieving for. They press close. Their amber eyes glow steadily in his presence. They know who he is, and they know where he is going, and their distress at the Citadel's direction intensifies when he stands among them, as though his presence makes the approaching confrontation real in a way it was not before.

*GM note: The Tamaron recruitment should not be a simple mechanical transaction. It is the party committing to the turning path — choosing to invest time and effort in the possibility that Baselia can be saved rather than proceeding directly to the Citadel for a combat confrontation. The time cost is real (the party loses at least a day, possibly more, during which no progress is made on the fifth stronghold), and the emotional cost is also real: Tamaron's presence on Nocturne is a constant reminder of the personal tragedy at the chapter's heart. If the party did not recruit Tamaron — either because he was killed on Illium, because they did not receive the clue about his importance, or because they chose not to make the trip — the Twin Cities serve their other function: the quiet before the storm, a moment to take stock of everything the party has seen and everything that remains. The difference between a party that arrives at the Citadel with Tamaron and a party that arrives without him is the difference between a chapter that ends in reunion and a chapter that ends in tragedy, and the GM should ensure that both paths feel earned.*

---

### Scene 8: Valley 5 — The Valley of Theater and Stronghold 5 — The Bargain

The fifth valley is the narrowest and deepest of the five — a slot canyon whose walls rise so steeply that the twilight reaches the valley floor only as a diffuse glow, the shadows deeper here than anywhere else on Nocturne. The architecture is sparse: a few small settlements clustered along the canyon floor, their buildings humble compared to the grand cities of the previous valleys, their function clearly residential rather than cultural. The Valley of Theater produced performers, not monuments — its art form was collaborative, transient, existing only in the moment of performance and the memory of the audience. The valley's physical infrastructure was always secondary to the human infrastructure of the Twin Cities' stages and workshops, and the settlements here have the character of dormitory towns: places where people lived between performances rather than places where culture was made.

The Citadel of Lament is visible at the valley's far end. Even at this distance — miles away, at the head of the canyon where the walls converge — its silhouette is unmistakable: a fortress of dark stone that rises from the mountain like an extension of the rock itself, its towers reaching higher than the canyon walls, its mass blocking the ambient light so that its shadow falls across the entire valley floor. The Citadel does not look like a seat of power. It looks like a place someone went to be alone with their grief, and built walls around it so the grief could not escape.

Between the party and the Citadel, at the mouth of the canyon where the valley begins to narrow, the fifth stronghold sits. It is the smallest of the five — not a fortress or a palace or a concert hall but a simple stone building, no larger than a modest house, its door open, its interior lit with a warm light that carries none of the deceptive glamour of Verithan's palace. The building looks, from the outside, like a place where someone lives. This is because someone does.

**The Fifth Spirit**

The spirit of the fifth stronghold is **Caeleth**, and he is the most complex and the most dangerous of the five — not in combat capability but in the thing he represents. The previous four spirits embodied the Cabal's various corruptions: Serenica's artistic ambition, Margolan's intellectual hunger, Korvellan's martial greed, Verithan's desire for control. Caeleth was the Cabal's philosopher. He joined the sorcerers not for power or knowledge or artistic transcendence but because he wanted to understand the nature of suffering — specifically, whether suffering could be eliminated from the mortal experience without destroying the capacity for joy that suffering makes possible. The Asura corruption reached him through this question, and the answer it provided was the Dream itself. Caeleth did not design the curse — that was a collective act, the Cabal's sorcerers working together under Asura influence — but his philosophical framework is the Dream's intellectual foundation. The idea that a population could be freed from suffering by being freed from change, that stasis could be a form of mercy, that the elimination of death and loss and the capacity for new experience could constitute salvation rather than damnation — this was Caeleth's contribution to the catastrophe, and he has had five centuries to consider whether he was right.

He has concluded that he was.

Caeleth manifests as a translucent Fetchling man of middle age, his appearance stable in a way that the other spirits' were not — no flickering, no dissolving, no shifts between living and dead selves. He looks, more than any other spirit the party has met, like a person: calm, composed, thoughtful, his expression carrying the settled quality of someone who has thought about something for a very long time and arrived at a position he is confident in. He is seated at a table when the party enters the stronghold. The orb sits on the table in front of him, unguarded, easily reachable. He gestures for the party to sit.

> *The interior of the stronghold is a single room. A table, chairs, a shelf of books, a window that looks out over the valley toward the distant shape of the Citadel. The spirit sits at the table with the orb in front of him the way a host might set out a bottle of wine for expected guests. He is the most human of the five spirits you have encountered — no visible strain, no flickering form, no signs of the madness or obsession that consumed the others. He looks at you with an expression of genuine welcome and something else, something you did not expect: curiosity. He wants to know who you are. Not what you can do for him. Who you are.*
>
> *"Please," he says, and the word carries a warmth that would be disarming if you had not spent four strongholds learning to distrust the gap between appearance and truth. "Sit. I have been thinking about what to say to you for a very long time, and I find that I would rather listen first."*

**The Bargain**

Caeleth offers the party the orb. Freely, unconditionally, with no strings attached — except one. He asks the party to leave the Dream intact.

His argument is not simple and should not be presented as such. Caeleth is the most intelligent and articulate being the party has encountered on Nocturne, and his position has been refined over five centuries of solitary contemplation. He does not argue that the Dream is good. He argues that the Dream is *better than the alternative*, and he makes his case with evidence the party has gathered themselves.

The Dream-bound population does not suffer. The party has seen this across four valleys: the musicians play with contentment, the scholars debate with enthusiasm, the sculptors maintain their works with pride, the painters study their murals with appreciation. The Fetchlings of Nocturne are not in pain. They are not aware of their loss. They do not grieve for the capacity they have been denied, because they cannot perceive its absence. The Dream, Caeleth argues, is not a prison — it is an anesthetic. It took away the thing that was destroying them (grief, loss, the knowledge of what the Cabal had done to their world) and replaced it with something tolerable. Is tolerable happiness less real than aware suffering?

Consider the alternative, he says. Break the Dream. Return the population to full mortality — to hunger, to fatigue, to the need for sleep, to the capacity for death that is not followed by reconstitution. Return them to the knowledge of what was taken from them. Five centuries of creative paralysis, five centuries of arguments that went nowhere, five centuries of unfinished sculptures and unwritten compositions and blank manuscript pages. The weight of that knowledge, delivered to a population that has no context for it, no preparation, no support — Caeleth argues that this is not liberation. It is cruelty. The Dream spares them the worst thing a conscious being can experience: the awareness of irreversible loss. Breaking it forces that awareness on millions of people who did nothing to deserve it.

And what will they gain? Caeleth asks. The ability to create again? Perhaps — if the Dream's breaking restores their generative capacity, which is not certain. The ability to die permanently? That is not a gift; that is the removal of a protection. The ability to perceive the truth? The truth is that their world was destroyed by sorcerers who thought they knew better, and breaking the Dream is simply another group of outsiders who think they know better making a decision that affects millions of people who were not consulted.

The party has the orb. They can take it and go. Caeleth does not threaten, does not bargain, does not attempt to extract a binding promise. He simply asks the party to consider what they are doing when they restore the final bridge and open the way to the Citadel. The bridges' restoration may or may not weaken the Dream — the mechanism is unclear, and Caeleth is honest about this uncertainty — but the trajectory is obvious. The party is dismantling the infrastructure that maintains the curse, and if the curse breaks, the consequences fall on a population that has no voice in the decision.

Caeleth's argument is self-serving in one respect, and the party should be allowed to identify this: he designed the Dream's philosophical framework, and its continuation validates his life's work. If the Dream is broken and the population suffers, he was wrong. If the Dream persists and the population remains content, he was right. He is not immune to this bias. He is honest about it if confronted — "Yes, I want to be right. I have wanted to be right for five centuries. That does not make me wrong." — and the honesty does not resolve the dilemma. He may be biased and correct simultaneously.

**The Choice**

The party can accept the bargain — take the orb without a fight, walk away with Caeleth's question ringing in their ears — or they can refuse it. Acceptance does not bind them to anything. The bargain is moral, not magical: Caeleth has no power to enforce it, no mechanism to punish the party if they break the Dream after promising not to. What he has is an argument, and the argument's power depends entirely on whether the party finds it compelling. A party that takes the orb and proceeds to the Citadel with the intention of turning Baselia and breaking the Dream has not violated any magical compact. They have simply chosen to disagree with a dead philosopher. Whether they feel good about that disagreement is between them and their consciences.

If the party refuses the bargain — if they tell Caeleth that the Dream must end, that the population deserves the truth regardless of the cost, that stasis is not mercy — Caeleth listens. He does not argue further. He stands, pushes the orb across the table toward them, and says, "Then take it. I hope you are right. I was not." He dissipates. The stronghold is empty. The orb is theirs.

If the party refuses the bargain and also chooses to fight — if they attack Caeleth rather than engaging with his argument — he fights, and he is the strongest of the five spirits in direct combat (CR 18). His abilities are rooted in the same philosophical framework that produced the Dream: enchantment magic that targets the will, auras that impose stasis on living creatures, and a capstone ability that forces a single target to experience the full weight of the Dream for 1d4 rounds (Will DC 24; on failure, the target perceives the world as the Dream-bound do — hollow, pleasant, devoid of urgency, all motivation and emotional intensity suppressed). He fights with reluctance and without malice, and if reduced below a quarter of his hit points he stops fighting, releases the orb, and dissipates with the same words: "I hope you are right." The combat path yields the same mechanical result as the diplomatic one. The difference is that the party chose violence against a being who was willing to give them what they wanted for free and only asked them to think about what they were doing.

*GM note: Stronghold 5 is the moral climax of the five-stronghold sequence, and it should be played with the weight that position demands. Caeleth's argument is designed to be genuinely compelling — not a villain's rationalization but a sincere philosophical position that the party may find difficult to dismiss. The GM should present his case fairly, without tipping the scales toward acceptance or refusal. There is no mechanically correct answer. Taking the orb and leaving the Dream intact is a valid choice that has consequences (the Dream persists even if Baselia is turned; the population remains frozen). Taking the orb and breaking the Dream is also a valid choice that has consequences (the population suffers the sudden onset of five centuries of repressed awareness). The party's decision here should inform the chapter's conclusion and the emotional tenor of the Citadel confrontation — a party that has wrestled with Caeleth's question arrives at Baselia's door with a different understanding of what they are fighting for than a party that simply took the orb and moved on.*

*One additional note: Caeleth's argument deliberately echoes Verithan's self-justification in Stronghold 4 — both argue that the population is better off not knowing the truth. The difference is that Verithan used this argument to justify personal cruelty (imprisoning Fetchlings for her own entertainment), while Caeleth uses it to justify inaction (leaving the Dream intact). The party should feel the resonance between the two positions and should be allowed to decide whether the difference in motivation makes the argument more or less persuasive when a philosopher rather than an abuser makes it.*

**Restoring the Fifth Bridge**

The fifth and final pylon stands at the canyon's narrowest point, where the Twin Cities face each other across the chasm. The orb seats itself, the channels ignite, and the bridge that blazes to life between the two halves of Dramara is the brightest and most sustained of the five — the light spanning the chasm with a warmth and intensity that speaks of a connection restored, a collaboration resumed, a severed artery reopened after five centuries of isolation.

> *The bridge ignites and the chasm fills with light. Not the single ribbon of the first bridge or the prismatic scatter of the fourth — this light is broad, warm, and steady, and it spans the gap between the Twin Cities the way a word spans the gap between two people who have not spoken in a very long time. The pylons on both sides blaze. The harmonic they produce is not a single tone but a chord — multiple frequencies blending, the acoustic properties of both cities combining for the first time in five centuries, the performance half and the production half singing together in a sound that neither could produce alone.*
>
> *In the near city, the opera house falls silent mid-performance. The singers stop. The orchestra stops. The audience turns, as one, toward the light. In the far city, the workshops go still. Tools are set down. Hands that have been maintaining costumes and building sets and repairing puppets for five hundred years are lowered to their sides. Both cities stare at the bridge that connects them — that has always connected them, in their architecture and their art and their purpose, even when the physical span was gone — and for a moment the Dream does not crack at its edges. It holds. The Fetchlings stare at the bridge with the same pleasant, hollow attention they bring to everything.*
>
> *Then a costumer in the far city picks up a bolt of fabric, walks to the bridge's edge, and stops. She stands there, the fabric held against her chest, looking across the span of light toward the opera house she can see on the far side. She does not cross. She does not put the fabric down. She stands at the threshold of a connection she has needed for five centuries and cannot remember needing, and the Dream holds her there — not preventing her from crossing, not quite, but failing to provide the impulse that would carry her the final step. She has the fabric. She has the bridge. She has the destination. She does not have the reason.*
>
> *She is still standing there when you leave.*

The way to the Citadel of Lament is open. All five bridges blaze behind the party — five ribbons of light connecting five valleys across chasms of absolute darkness, the magitek infrastructure of a civilization beginning, for the first time in five centuries, to function as a connected system rather than five isolated fragments. The Citadel looms at the head of Valley 5, its dark stone absorbing the twilight, its towers rising above the canyon walls, its shadow reaching toward the party like a hand extended in greeting or in warning.

*GM note: The fifth bridge restoration is the last and should be the most emotionally resonant. The previous four bridges cracked the Dream at its edges — moments of almost-awareness, flickers of grief, hands that trembled. The fifth bridge completes the physical infrastructure but does not break the Dream, and the costumer standing at the bridge's edge with her fabric is the image the chapter offers of what remains undone. The party has restored the connections. They have not restored the people. That requires what happens at the Citadel — either Baselia's turning, which begins the slow process of the Dream's dissolution, or Baselia's death, which leaves the Dream intact and the costumer standing at the bridge's edge forever. The GM should let the image land. The costumer is not a named NPC, not a quest objective, not a character with dialogue. She is a person standing at the edge of the thing she needs, held back by a curse she cannot see, and she is every Fetchling on Nocturne in a single figure.*

---

### Scene 9: The Citadel of Lament

The approach to the Citadel takes the party through the narrowing slot canyon of Valley 5, past the dormitory settlements whose Fetchlings watch them go with the same placid attention the Dream-bound bring to everything, past the empty stronghold where Caeleth sat, and into the deepening shadow beneath the canyon walls as they converge toward the fortress at the valley's head. The twilight, which has been a constant companion since the party's arrival — violet-grey, diffuse, beautiful in its haunted way — fails here. The canyon walls are too steep, the gap too narrow, and the Citadel's mass blocks what little ambient light reaches this deep. The darkness should be absolute. It is not.

Above the Citadel, the sky burns.

The aurora appears as the party draws within a mile of the fortress — or perhaps it has always been there, hidden by the canyon walls until the angle of approach reveals it. It fills the sky above the Citadel in curtains of light that have no right to exist on a world without a sun to drive them: vast, luminous sheets of color that shift and fold and ripple in a wind that blows at altitudes no weather touches. The colors are wrong. Not the prismatic spectrum of the Rainbow Road or the warm golden light of the restored bridges — these are the colors of something sacred that has been inverted, greens and violets and deep, bruised reds that pulse with a rhythm too slow and too regular to be natural, as though the aurora is breathing. The light it casts is sufficient to illuminate the land around the party in shifting, uncertain color, turning the dark stone of the canyon walls into something that alternates between beautiful and terrible depending on which band of light is dominant. In the green phases the stone looks almost alive, the shadows soft and the texture of the rock rich with detail. In the red phases the same stone looks wounded, the shadows harsh, the texture of the rock slick and organic.

Shapes coalesce in the aurora. They are visible only at the edges of attention — look directly and the curtains of light are curtains of light, nothing more, but look away and the peripheral vision catches forms assembling and dissolving in the luminous folds. Figures. Not specific enough to identify, not sustained enough to study, but unmistakably figures — humanoid shapes that gather and reach and fall apart, their movements suggesting a narrative the eye cannot quite follow. The shapes are not threatening. They are not comforting. They are the residue of something that happened here five centuries ago — the moment Baselia's divine power inverted, the moment a powerful paladin's connection to the gods was severed and replaced by something else — and the aurora is the visible scar of that inversion, the corrupted divine energy radiating from the Citadel in bands of light that the sky cannot absorb and cannot disperse.

> *The sky above the Citadel is on fire. Not with flame — with light that moves like flame, curtains of it folding and unfolding across the darkness in colors that your eyes accept but your instincts reject. Green that shifts to violet. Violet that deepens to a red so dark it is almost black. The light pulses with a rhythm you can feel in your sternum, slow and deliberate, the heartbeat of something vast and wounded. It illuminates the land around you in shifting color — the dark stone of the canyon painted green, then violet, then red, the shadows swinging with each change like the hands of a clock measuring something other than time.*
>
> *You see shapes in the light. You cannot see them when you look directly — the aurora is simply light, beautiful and strange and nothing more — but when your gaze shifts, when you look at the stone or the path or each other, the edges of your vision catch them. Figures. They form in the luminous curtains the way faces form in clouds: gradually, unmistakably, and then they are gone. They reach upward, or toward each other, or toward something below them — toward the Citadel itself — and then the light shifts and they dissolve, and the aurora is simply light again, and you are not certain what you saw.*
>
> *The Citadel of Lament rises ahead of you, its dark stone drinking the aurora's shifting color the way every surface on Nocturne drinks the twilight. Its towers are the highest structures you have seen on this world — higher than the canyon walls, higher than the peaks that frame the valleys — and they are built not for defense or habitation but for height itself, as though their architect wanted to reach the sky and failed. The aurora bends around the towers. The shapes that form and dissolve in its folds are denser here, more frequent, and though you still cannot look at them directly you have the growing conviction that they are looking at you.*

**The Approach**

The Citadel was not built as a military installation. Its walls are thick and its gates are heavy, but its architecture lacks the calculated defensibility of Korvellan's redoubt — there are no murder holes, no overlapping fields of fire, no killing grounds designed to channel attackers into disadvantageous positions. The Citadel was built as a residence, and its defenses are an afterthought imposed by someone who wanted to be left alone and had the power to ensure it. The gates are sealed by Baselia's will rather than by locks or mechanisms — the dark iron doors respond to her authority and to nothing else, though sufficient force (Strength DC 30, or appropriate magic such as *knock* at CL 18, *disintegrate*, or *mythic power*) can breach them.

The Citadel's undead guardians patrol the exterior grounds and the interior corridors. They are not the mindless shambling dead of lesser necromancers — Baselia's corrupted divine power has produced guardians that retain a shadow of the martial discipline they possessed in life. They were her paladins once, the warriors who served under her banner before the corruption took her, and their undead forms still wear the armor and carry the weapons of their former stations. They fight in formation. They respond to tactical developments. They hold positions and withdraw in order when overmatched. They do not speak, and their eyes — dark, empty, lit from within by the same aurora-light that fills the sky above — carry no recognition and no mercy. There are approximately thirty guardians distributed across the Citadel's exterior and interior, organized in squads of five.

For mechanical purposes, treat each undead guardian as a Graveknight Cavalier (CR 11) with the following modifications: remove the mount, reduce speed to 30 ft., and add channel resistance +4 (reflecting the power of the anti-paladin who created them). They are vulnerable to positive energy and to effects that specifically target undead. In squads of five, they present a significant but manageable threat to a level 17 mythic party — the real danger is their numbers and their coordination, not their individual power. A party that fights through the full complement is spending resources they may need for the confrontation with Baselia herself.

**With Tamaron Present**

If Tamaron accompanies the party, the approach to the Citadel changes fundamentally. Tamaron's slowly-returning divine power — unreliable in most contexts, inconsistent in its manifestation — responds to the Citadel's undead guardians with a clarity and force it has not displayed since his liberation. He channels positive energy as the party advances, and the effect is devastating: the guardians that were his comrades in another life recoil from the light he produces, their formations breaking, their discipline failing. Several of them — the oldest, the ones who retain the deepest shadow of who they were — stop fighting entirely. They lower their weapons. They stand motionless as Tamaron passes, and if the aurora's light catches them at the right angle, the party may see something in their dead eyes that looks like recognition. They remember their commander. They cannot act on the memory, but they cannot fight him either.

With Tamaron, the guardian encounters are reduced in difficulty by approximately half — not because Tamaron is a powerful combatant (he is not, in his diminished state) but because his presence disrupts the guardians' coherence. The party reaches the inner citadel having spent fewer resources and in a fundamentally different emotional state: they have watched a broken man walk through the ranks of warriors who once served him, watched the dead recognize the living, and they understand in a visceral way that the corruption they have come to break was not an abstract curse but a specific destruction of specific relationships between specific people.

The magitek horse constructs, if the party brought them to the Citadel, refuse to enter the fortress. They stop at the gates, their ears flat, their amber eyes dim, their bodies trembling with a distress the party has only seen in muted form during the journey through the valleys. The constructs will wait outside. They will not go in. Whatever they sense inside — the inversion of the power they were built to serve, the corruption of the woman they loved — it is more than they can bear to approach. If Baselia is turned, the constructs enter the Citadel on their own, without prompting, the moment the corruption lifts. If she is killed, they remain at the gates, motionless, for a very long time.

**The Throne Room**

The Citadel's heart is a great hall whose proportions echo the opera house in the Twin Cities — the same tiered arrangement, the same orientation toward a central performance space — but rendered in dark iron and darker stone, lit by the aurora's light filtering through narrow windows high in the walls. The central space is occupied by a stage. On the stage, the dead perform.

Baselia's macabre performances are the final expression of the Dream's logic applied to a mind that is not Dream-bound but has arrived at the same destination through different means. The undead and bound spirits of slain Cabal sorcerers — not the five stronghold spirits, who held their positions and their orbs, but lesser members of the Cabal, sorcerers Baselia killed during her initial purge — are compelled to enact the creative works that Nocturne once produced. They perform operas. They stage plays. They dance in formations choreographed five centuries ago for living performers whose grace and intention the dead cannot replicate. The performances are technically accomplished in the way that a mechanical reproduction of music is technically accomplished — every note is correct, every step is placed, and nothing that made the art meaningful survives the translation. The dead do not interpret. They execute. The result is a grotesque mirror of the Dream-bound population's frozen routines: where the Fetchlings in the valleys maintain their art out of hollow contentment, the dead in the Citadel maintain it out of compulsion, and neither knows the difference.

Baselia watches from a throne of dark iron on a raised dais at the hall's far end. She has been watching for five centuries.

> *The hall opens before you in dark iron and the aurora's shifting light. The windows are high and narrow and the colors that pass through them sweep the floor in bands — green, violet, red — that move across the stone the way searchlights move across a battlefield. At the hall's center, on a stage that could hold an orchestra, the dead perform. You recognize opera — the staging, the blocked positions, the gesture language of the form — but the performers are hollow. Their mouths open and sounds emerge that are technically correct and mean nothing. Their bodies move through choreography that was designed for living grace and is executed with the precision of machinery. The performance is immaculate and it is the most disturbing thing you have seen on Nocturne, worse than the Dream-bound population's hollow contentment because this is not contentment — this is compulsion, and the things that are compelled were people once, and the person who compels them sits at the far end of the hall on a throne of dark iron and watches with an expression that you struggle to name until you realize it is the same expression the Dream-bound wear when they listen to music or tend their gardens or stand before blank walls they cannot fill.*
>
> *She is not Dream-bound. But she has found her way to the same place.*
>
> *The aurora's light catches her. She is Fetchling — grey-skinned, sharp-featured, her frame lean and hard beneath armor that was once a paladin's plate and is now something else, the metal darkened to near-black, the holy symbols that once adorned it defaced or inverted. Her eyes glow with the same corrupted light that fills the sky above her fortress. She looks old — not in the way of aged mortals but in the way of stone that has been weathered past its tolerance, eroded rather than decayed, worn down by five centuries of grief that has no outlet and no end. She sees you. The dead on the stage continue their performance. She does not dismiss them. She does not stand. She watches you approach with the focused attention of someone who has been expecting this moment for a very long time and is not certain whether it is a relief or a final cruelty.*

**The Turning Path**

This section applies only if Tamaron is present — alive, turned on Illium, recruited by the party, and brought physically to the Citadel. If all four conditions are met, the confrontation with Baselia is not combat. It is the most difficult conversation in the campaign.

Tamaron steps forward. Baselia sees him. The dead on the stage falter — not stopping, but losing their rhythm, the compulsion that drives them disrupted by the spike of emotion that tears through Baselia's control when she recognizes the man standing in her hall. She stands. The throne of dark iron groans as she rises from it. The aurora's light intensifies — the shapes in the curtains above the Citadel become denser, more urgent, as though the corrupted energy that sustains Baselia is responding to the threat of its own dissolution.
