What follows is not scripted. The GM should play this scene with Baselia and Tamaron as fully realized characters, not as mechanical components of a turning system. There are no levers to pull, no locks to open, no mindscape battle to fight. There is a woman who was betrayed by the man she loved, who was broken by his abandonment, who turned to dark powers in her desperation to save her people and destroyed them instead, and who has spent five centuries watching the dead perform the art of the living because it is the only way she can remember what she lost. And there is a man who abandoned her, who retreated into solitary penance rather than facing the consequences of his actions, who was captured and possessed by the very forces his cowardice left unchecked, and who has now walked into her fortress — broken, diminished, barely capable of standing — because he owes her this, and because he loves her, and because love that was not strong enough to prevent a catastrophe must at least be strong enough to stand in front of it and say so.

The conversation is ugly. Baselia's first reaction is rage — five centuries of compressed fury erupting at the sight of the man who caused all of this by leaving. She does not attack him physically (the party should not need to restrain her), but her words are weapons that she wields with the same precision she once brought to her sword: every failure enumerated, every promise broken, every consequence of his abandonment laid at his feet with the merciless specificity of someone who has rehearsed this speech for half a millennium. Tamaron takes it. He does not defend himself. He does not explain. He stands in the aurora's shifting light and lets her say everything she has needed to say since the day he left, and the only thing he offers in response — when she runs out of words and stands trembling in the silence that follows — is the truth: "I failed you. I am here."

Baselia does not believe she can be forgiven. She says so — not as a rhetorical position but as a statement of fact, delivered with the certainty of a woman who has cataloged her sins with the same obsessive precision she once brought to her faith. She killed the Cabal sorcerers. She cast the spell that became the Dream. She watched her people die and reconstitute and forget and she could not stop it and she could not fix it and eventually she stopped trying and sat on a throne of dark iron and watched the dead perform because it was the only thing she had left. Forgiveness is for people who made mistakes. She made a holocaust.

Tamaron's response is the scene's fulcrum, and the GM should deliver it with the weight it demands. He does not forgive her. He does not have the right. What he says — what the GM must find the words for, in whatever form best suits the table — is that forgiveness is not the point. The point is that the woman who sits on that throne and watches the dead perform is not the woman he loved. The woman he loved would have burned the throne and freed the dead and walked out of this fortress five centuries ago, and the fact that she did not means that the curse took her too — not through the Dream, which cannot touch her, but through the grief that the Dream was supposed to prevent and instead made permanent. She tried to save her people from suffering and she succeeded, and the price was that she absorbed all the suffering they could not feel, and the weight of it crushed her into this. She is not an anti-paladin because she chose evil. She is an anti-paladin because grief inverted everything she was, and the inversion was so complete that she cannot see the way back.

Tamaron can see it. He is standing in it.

The turning is not a dramatic moment of radiant light and divine restoration. It is Baselia sitting down — not on the throne, on the floor, on the dark stone of the dais — and putting her face in her hands. The armor she wears does not shatter or transform. The aurora above the Citadel does not vanish. The dead on the stage do not collapse. What happens is smaller and more significant: Baselia stops. The compulsion that drives the dead performers ceases, and they stand motionless on the stage, empty shells waiting for a command that does not come. The aurora's light dims — not extinguished but softened, the bruised reds fading, the colors shifting toward something less wounded. The shapes that coalesce in the curtains of light slow and still and, for the first time, hold their forms long enough for the party to see what they have always been: the people Baselia lost. Her paladins, her subjects, the population she tried to save. They are not ghosts. They are memories, projected into the sky by a divine power so corrupted by grief that it could not stop mourning even when its bearer no longer had the words for what she mourned. The shapes hold for a long moment. Then they dissolve, and the aurora fades to a dim glow, and the Citadel is quiet.

Tamaron sits down beside her. He does not touch her. He does not speak. He is there. After five centuries, he is there.

*GM note: The turning scene is the emotional climax of the chapter and one of the campaign's most important moments. The GM should give it time and space. There is no mechanical resolution — no dice rolled, no DCs set, no ability scores compared. The turning happens because Tamaron is there and because what he represents — the possibility that the person Baselia was still exists beneath the person she became — is sufficient to crack the armor she has built around herself. The party's role is witness. They do not need to speak, persuade, or act. They brought Tamaron here. That was their contribution. The rest is between two people who loved each other and failed each other and are now, at the end of everything, sitting on a stone floor in a dark fortress, not touching, not speaking, and beginning — barely, tentatively, against five centuries of evidence that it is not possible — to find a way back to each other. Let the scene breathe. Let the players feel it. Then move on.*

**The Combat Path**

This section applies if Tamaron is dead, if Tamaron was not recruited, or if the party chooses combat. In all three cases, Baselia cannot be turned. The confrontation is a fight.

**If Tamaron was not recruited (alive but absent):** Baselia engages the party with words before weapons. She is not mindless — she is aware of what she has become, aware of what the Dream has done to her people, and aware that the party has restored the bridges and cleared the strongholds. She speaks to them from the throne with a composure that is worse than rage because it is genuine: she has made her peace with what she is, and she does not believe that anything the party has done — or could do — changes the fundamental equation. The Dream persists. Her people are trapped. She is trapped. The only question is whether the party can make it stop, and she does not believe they can — not without Tamaron, not without the one person whose presence could reach her. If the party mentions Tamaron, her composure cracks. The crack is visible — a flinch, a tightening of the jaw, a flare of the aurora through the high windows — and then it seals. "He is not here," she says. "If he wanted to be here, he would be here." The logic is wrong. She does not care. She draws her sword.

**If Tamaron is dead:** Baselia knows. She felt it when it happened — the severing of a connection she had carried for five centuries, the sudden absence of the one person whose existence gave her suffering a shape. His death did not break her — she was already broken — but it removed the last possibility that anything could be different. She engages the party with the focused intensity of someone who has nothing left to protect and nothing left to lose. She does not waste words. She does not monologue. She says Tamaron's name once — quietly, to herself, before the first swing — and then she fights.

Baselia's full stat block is in the appendix (see Stat Block Appendix, Lady Sorrow / Baselia the Undaunted — CR 18). The key tactical elements of the fight:

**The Throne Room Battlefield.** The hall is large enough that positioning matters. The dead performers on the stage are environmental obstacles — they do not fight, but they occupy space and they do not move unless Baselia commands them to (as a free action, she can direct the dead to clear the stage or to form a wall of bodies that provides soft cover). The dais is elevated, giving Baselia higher ground (+1 to melee attacks). The aurora's light creates shifting illumination that imposes a 20% miss chance on ranged attacks made from more than 30 feet (the colors shift unpredictably, creating momentary visual distortions). The high windows can be shattered to admit more light, reducing the miss chance to 10% but also increasing the intensity of the aurora's effect on those below (Fort DC 18 each round or be dazzled for 1 round by the raw display).

**Baselia's Fighting Style.** She fights as a fallen paladin — disciplined, economical, and devastatingly effective. Her Smite Good targets the party's strongest divine-aligned character first (she can sense alignment as per *detect good*, at will). Her Aura of Despair (10-foot radius, -2 penalty to all saving throws) makes her dangerous to engage in melee. Her Touch of Corruption — channeled through her sword rather than her hands — adds negative energy damage to every hit and can nauseate targets that fail their saves. She fights to kill, not to perform. There is no dramatic posturing, no theatrical villain combat. She is a professional warrior with five centuries of practice and a divine power source that has been fueling her fury since the day Tamaron left.

**The Undead Reinforcements.** If the party dispatched the corridor guardians on the way in, no reinforcements arrive. If any guardians survived (or if the party bypassed them), they converge on the throne room 3 rounds after combat begins — up to three squads of five, arriving from different entrances. Tamaron's presence (turning path) would have neutralized most of these; his absence means the party may face Baselia and her remaining guardians simultaneously.

**Baselia's Final Stand.** When reduced below 50 hit points, Baselia activates her Grief Unbounded ability — a burst of corrupted divine energy that fills the throne room (60-foot radius, Will DC 24). Creatures that fail the save experience a fraction of Baselia's accumulated grief: five centuries of loss, compressed into a single moment of psychic anguish. The effect is 10d6 psychic damage and staggered for 1d4 rounds. Creatures that succeed take half damage and are not staggered. The ability can be used once. Its use triggers a visible change in the aurora above the Citadel — the lights flare, the shapes in the curtains reach downward toward the fortress, and the air in the throne room fills with a sound that is not quite music and not quite weeping but partakes of both.

When Baselia falls, the death is not triumphant. She drops to one knee, then to both. Her sword falls from her hand. The aurora above the Citadel flares once — a final pulse of wounded light — and then begins to fade, not extinguishing but diminishing, the colors cooling, the shapes dissolving for the last time. Baselia looks at the party with eyes that are, for one moment, clear of the corrupted glow that has sustained her. The clarity lasts long enough for her to speak.

"Tell him —" she says. And then the clarity is gone, and so is she.

If Tamaron is dead, the sentence is unfinished and unfinishable. If Tamaron is alive but absent, the party carries a message from a dead woman to a man who could have saved her, and the weight of that message is the chapter's final cost.

**Corruption: +2.** Baselia's death adds 2 to the campaign corruption score. If Tamaron was also killed on Illium (+3), the combined corruption from the Illium-Nocturne chain is +5 — the most severe consequence of any decision sequence in the campaign.

*GM note: The combat path should feel like a tragedy, not a victory. The party is killing a woman who was destroyed by grief — grief for her people, grief for the man who left her, grief for the paladin she was and could not remain. She is powerful and dangerous and she will kill party members if the party is careless, but the emotional register of the fight should never be triumphant. The aurora above the Citadel — the visible expression of her corrupted mourning — makes the stakes visible: those shapes in the light are the people she lost, projected into the sky by a power that could not stop grieving. When the party strikes her down, they are not defeating evil. They are ending a five-century-long breakdown that no one came to interrupt until it was too late. "Tell him —" should be the last thing the party hears. The sentence is never finished. The GM should not decide what she was going to say. Neither should the party. The unfinished sentence is the point.*

---

### Scene 10: The Womb of Darkness

With Baselia turned or dead, the sealed vault beneath the Citadel can be accessed. The entrance is in the floor of the throne room, behind the dais — a stairway of dark stone descending into the mountain, its walls bare, its air cold and still. If Baselia was turned, she opens the seal herself — a gesture that costs her visible effort, the corrupted power that locked the vault now resisting its own user as her alignment shifts. The seal breaks with a sound like a chain snapping under tension, and the stairway is open. If Baselia was killed, the seal must be forced: *dispel magic* (CL 20), *break enchantment* (CL 18), *mythic power* expenditure, or raw force (Strength DC 35, or appropriate siege-level magic). The seal is powerful but not permanent — it was designed to keep the curious out, not to withstand a determined assault by a mythic party.

The descent is long — hundreds of steps, carved with the same precision as the Thousand Steps that led to the Old Man's shrine, but spiraling downward rather than upward, into the mountain's roots. The aurora's light does not reach here. The darkness is absolute and natural, the first true darkness the party has encountered on Nocturne — not the twilight that defines the surface but a genuine absence of light, the mountain's interior sealed from every external source of illumination. The party must provide their own light, and the light they carry behaves strangely: it does not reflect from the walls in the expected way, producing no shadows, no highlights, no sense of depth. The stairway feels infinite until it ends.

The vault is a single chamber at the base of the stairway — a high-ceilinged space of natural stone, unworked, the first surface on Nocturne that has not been carved or painted or acoustically calibrated. The chamber is ancient in a way that the surface constructions are not, old enough that the stone itself has the quality of something that was here before the mountain formed around it. At the chamber's center, suspended in the air at the height of a tall man's chest, the Womb of Darkness hangs.

> *The chamber opens at the base of the stairs and you understand immediately that you have passed out of Baselia's domain and into something older. The walls are raw stone — the first unworked surface you have seen on this world, the first place where no hand has shaped the rock or marked it with art. The air is different here. Not cold but absent — temperature has no meaning in this space, and neither does distance, and neither does time, though you become aware of these absences only gradually, the way you become aware of silence only after the noise has stopped.*
>
> *At the chamber's center, an orb of darkness hangs in the air. It is not dark in the way that shadows are dark — it is dark in the way that a closed eye is dark, the darkness of something internal rather than external, the darkness of a space that light has never entered because it was never meant to. The orb is perhaps three feet across. Its surface — if it has a surface — is perfectly smooth and perfectly still and perfectly black, and looking at it produces a sensation that is not visual but conceptual: the understanding that what you are seeing is not an object but an opening, and that the opening leads somewhere that is not a place.*
>
> *The orb waits. It has been waiting for a very long time. It is patient in the way that the deep stone is patient, and the silence that surrounds it is the silence of something that knows you will come to it when you are ready.*

**Entering the Womb**

Passing through the orb transports the entrant to a space beyond conventional reality — not a demiplane or an extraplanar location but something more fundamental, a place that exists in the relationship between consciousness and the void that preceded it. Time does not function inside the Womb. A person who enters may experience moments or years of subjective time while only a fraction of a second passes in the material world. The Womb cannot be entered involuntarily — it requires an act of will, a deliberate choice to step into the darkness — and it cannot be escaped involuntarily either. The entrant leaves when they choose to leave, and the choice is always available.

Inside the Womb, thoughts take on ghostly physical dimensions. Memories become visible: translucent, three-dimensional recreations of past events that the entrant can observe from any angle, walk through, examine with a clarity that surpasses the original experience. Emotions manifest as environmental conditions — grief produces a cold rain, joy produces warmth and light, fear produces shadow, resolve produces solid ground beneath the feet. The entrant's own nature is laid bare: every decision they have made, every consequence that followed, every path they chose and every path they rejected is available for examination with perfect, unflinching clarity. The experience is not punitive. The Womb does not judge. It reflects, and the reflection is precise enough that the entrant must judge themselves.

Each party member who enters the Womb experiences something different — the visions are personal, shaped by the entrant's own history and the choices they have made during the campaign. The GM should tailor these experiences to the specific characters at the table, drawing on the party's accumulated decisions across eight worlds. A character who killed a Warlock sees the Warlock's life before corruption, the moment the choice was made, and the consequence that followed. A character who turned a Warlock sees the same — but also sees the Warlock's future, the slow work of rebuilding, the person they are becoming. A character who carries guilt sees it clearly, without distortion, and must decide what to do with the clarity. A character who carries purpose sees the source of that purpose, and whether it will survive what is coming.

The Womb's power is introspection — the mythic capability to confront one's own nature with absolute honesty and emerge strengthened rather than destroyed by the confrontation. This is the power of mythic tier 8, and it settles into the party not as a burst of divine energy or a flash of golden light but as a quiet, settled certainty: they know who they are. They know what they have done. They know what remains to be done. The certainty is not comfortable — it includes every failure, every compromise, every cost — but it is complete, and completeness, at this stage of the journey, is its own form of power.

**The Eighth Fragment of the Song of Heaven**

The Song's eighth fragment reveals itself inside the Womb — not learned in the conventional sense but discovered, as though it has always been part of the Song and the party is only now capable of hearing it. The fragment's theme is **Memory**, and its nature is paradox.

The Song of Heaven, the party now understands, is not merely a mechanism for opening the Rainbow Road. It is a record. Every world the party has visited, every choice they have made, every Warlock they have turned or killed — the Song remembers all of it. The eight fragments they carry contain within their harmonics the preserved essence of eight worlds: Tanis's wild growth, Vatra's industrial fire, Illium's golden perfection, Nocturne's haunted twilight, and every world before and between. The Song does not merely connect the Nine Worlds. It *remembers* them. It holds them in its structure the way the Dream holds Nocturne's population — preserved, sustained, maintained against the entropy that would otherwise erase them.

The parallel to the Dream is deliberate and devastating. The Song's preservation is purposeful — it maintains the connections between worlds so that life can flow between them. The Dream's preservation is purposeless — it maintains a population in stasis so that nothing can change. The eighth fragment is the fragment that draws this distinction: memory without release is the Dream. Release without memory is oblivion. The Song walks the line between them, and the eighth fragment asks whether the party walks it too. What have they chosen to preserve? What have they chosen to release? Are they singing to hold on to what was, or to build what will be?

The answer, the fragment suggests, is both. Memory and release are not opposites. They are complements — the twin functions of a consciousness capable of learning from the past without being imprisoned by it. The Dream failed because it preserved without purpose. The Song succeeds because it preserves with purpose — and the purpose is not stasis but continuity, the capacity to carry forward what matters while releasing what does not.

> *The Song rises. You do not sing it — it sings itself, or the Womb sings it, or the darkness that is not darkness remembers it and lets it go. The eighth fragment is the sound of something being set down — not dropped, not discarded, but deliberately, carefully placed, the way you set down a weight you have carried so long that your arms have forgotten what it feels like to be empty. The fragment is Memory. It is the sound of everything you have seen since you first stepped onto the Rainbow Road — every world, every face, every choice, every consequence — and it is also the sound of everything you have not yet done, the worlds ahead, the choices unmade, the Song's final fragment still waiting to be found. Memory without release is the Dream. Release without memory is oblivion. The Song holds both, and the eighth fragment is the note where holding and releasing become the same act.*

**If Baselia is Present**

If Baselia was turned, she enters the Womb. She does not ask permission. She does not hesitate. She walks to the orb of darkness, studies it for a moment with an expression that is no longer the anti-paladin's controlled composure but something rawer and more uncertain — the expression of a woman who has spent five centuries avoiding the interior of her own mind and is now choosing to enter it — and steps through.

What Baselia experiences inside the Womb is hers alone. The party does not see it. When she emerges — moments later in material time, though the set of her shoulders and the depth of her eyes suggest that the subjective experience was considerably longer — she is changed. Not healed. Healing will take years, and the Womb does not heal. What the Womb provides is clarity, and the clarity that Baselia carries out of the darkness is the unobstructed view of everything she did and everything it cost, seen without the distortion of corruption or the anesthetic of despair. She has faced it. She has not flinched. She is standing.

Tamaron is waiting at the chamber's entrance. The constructs are waiting at the Citadel's gates. The aurora above the Citadel, when Baselia climbs the stairs and steps into the open air, has faded to a gentle luminescence — no longer the bruised, pulsing display of corrupted grief but a soft, steady glow, violet and silver, the colors of Nocturne's natural twilight reflected in the sky. The shapes are gone. The sky is clear. Baselia looks up at it, and for the first time in five centuries, she does not see the dead. She sees the sky.

*GM note: The Womb of Darkness is the chapter's final internal moment before the external conclusion. It should be played quietly, with weight, and with attention to each party member's individual experience. The mythic tier 8 advancement is not a reward for defeating Baselia — it is a reward for the journey through Nocturne, for the five valleys and five strongholds and the accumulated understanding of what the Dream means and what it costs. The party emerges from the Womb carrying the Song's eighth fragment and the knowledge that the Song itself is a kind of memory — a living record of every world they have visited and every choice they have made. This knowledge is important for the final chapters: the Song is not merely a tool. It is the thing that holds the Nine Worlds together, and completing it is not a mechanical act but an act of remembrance, a declaration that the worlds matter and the connections between them are worth preserving. The party should leave the Womb feeling that they understand, for the first time, what they are actually doing when they sing.*

---

### Chapter Conclusion

**Milestone: Level 18 and Mythic Tier 8.** Awarded after the Womb of Darkness. The party has completed Nocturne — the eighth of the Nine Worlds — and they carry eight of the Song of Heaven's nine fragments. One world remains.

---

**World State: Baselia Turned**

The Dream begins to weaken. The process is not instantaneous and not painless — Baselia's turning did not cast a counter-spell or trigger a mechanical dispelling. What it did was break the engine that sustained the curse: Baselia's corrupted divine power, which had been feeding the Dream for five centuries, is no longer corrupted, and without that power source the Dream begins to lose coherence the way a fire loses heat when the fuel is withdrawn. The weakening is gradual. Over the days and weeks following the party's departure, the Dream-bound Fetchlings begin to experience what they have not experienced in five centuries: change.

The change is not kind. The Fetchlings' lost memories do not return — five centuries of death, reconstitution, and erasure cannot be undone — but the capacity for new memories reasserts itself, and with it comes the capacity for new experience, which includes the capacity for suffering. The population must relearn hunger. They must relearn fatigue. They must relearn the need for sleep, the awareness of aging, and the finality of death — all the mortal conditions that the Dream removed and that their bodies have not experienced in five hundred years. The adjustment is brutal. Some Fetchlings respond with terror. Others respond with grief — not for what they lost, which they cannot remember, but for the comfort of the Dream itself, the hollow contentment that is now, for the first time, recognizable as hollow. The musician Thessaly puts down her instrument mid-phrase and cannot remember why she was playing. The archivist Caelan looks at his blank intake forms and, for the first time, understands that they have always been blank. The composer Mirel sits at her desk, stares at the empty pages that surround her, and weeps — not because she cannot write, but because she can feel, for the first time, the weight of the centuries she spent not writing, and the feeling is the worst thing she has ever experienced.

But: the painter standing before the blank wall in Chromara has not moved. Her hand is still raised. Her brush is still shaking. And as the Dream loosens its grip — not today, not this week, but soon, inevitably, as the curse's power bleeds away and the capacity for creation reasserts itself in the minds it held frozen — she will make a mark. The first new work of art produced on Nocturne in five centuries will be a single brushstroke on a bare stone wall, imperfect and uncertain, made by a woman who does not remember learning to paint but whose hands remember the motion even if her mind does not. It is a small thing. It is the most significant cultural event in the realm's history.

Baselia and Tamaron remain on Nocturne. Their relationship is not restored — five centuries of separation, mutual failure, and the accumulated damage of corruption and possession cannot be undone by a single conversation on a stone floor. They are not lovers. They are not yet friends. They are two people who destroyed each other and who have now, against every reasonable expectation, chosen to build something from the wreckage rather than walk away from it. The work ahead of them is immense: a population emerging from a five-century dream, a magitek infrastructure in need of full restoration, a culture that must rediscover creativity from first principles. Baselia has the authority and the knowledge. Tamaron has the faith and the endurance. Together they are not sufficient. Together they are a beginning.

The aurora above the Citadel fades to nothing over the course of the following weeks. The sky above the fortress returns to Nocturne's natural twilight — violet-grey, beautiful, no longer wounded. The shapes do not return. Baselia no longer needs to project her grief into the sky. She carries it with her, where it belongs, and the carrying is survivable.

**Nexus Contribution: Turned.** Baselia provides Nocturne's military strength to the alliance: Fetchling shadow-warriors, the remnants of her retinue now returned to their original oaths, and Baselia herself. She is not yet a full paladin — the divine connection severed five centuries ago has begun to return but is fragile and inconsistent — but her martial skill is undiminished and her motivation is renewed. She fights with the ferocity of someone who has been given a second chance and does not intend to waste it. The magitek horse constructs join the alliance's mounted forces, their loyalty to the party extending to the party's cause. Nocturne's contribution is significant: shadow-warriors who fight with the disciplined coordination of the undead guardians the party encountered in the Citadel, but alive and willing, their skills honed by centuries of Dream-preserved training now directed by conscious choice.

---

**World State: Baselia Killed**

The Dream persists. Without Baselia's turning, the curse has no clean resolution — the engine that sustains it is destroyed (Baselia's corrupted divine power died with her), but the Dream's momentum carries it forward like a wheel that continues to spin after the hand that pushed it is removed. The weakening is far slower than in the turning path, measured in decades rather than weeks, and the population shows no sign of emerging from its grip during the timeframe of the campaign. The Fetchlings of the five valleys continue their hollow routines: the musicians play, the scholars debate, the sculptors polish, the painters maintain, the performers perform. The bridges blaze. The valleys are connected. The Cabal spirits are gone. And the people are still frozen, cheerful and hollow and unaware, because the party killed the only person who could have broken the curse cleanly and the Dream does not care about bridges or orbs or the intentions of outsiders.

The Citadel of Lament is empty. The undead guardians, released by Baselia's death, collapse where they stand — the corrupted divine power that animated them is gone, and what remains is armor and bones and the fading echo of the people they were before Baselia raised them. The macabre performances end. The dead on the stage stop mid-note, mid-step, mid-gesture, and are still. The throne of dark iron sits empty. The aurora above the Citadel dims over the following hours and extinguishes entirely by the next twilight-dawn — not fading gradually, as in the turning path, but going out, the way a fire goes out when there is nothing left to burn. The shapes that formed in its folds are gone. They were Baselia's grief made visible, and the grief died with her.

The costumer in Dramara is still standing at the bridge's edge with her bolt of fabric. She will stand there for a very long time.

**Nexus Contribution: Killed.** Minimal. Some Fetchlings answer the call to the alliance — those the party freed from Verithan's palace in Stronghold 4, those in Sonoria and Lithara and Lexara who saw the bridges restored and felt the first cracks in the Dream's hold. Their numbers are small, their organization nonexistent, their combat capability limited. Without Baselia's leadership, Nocturne's military contribution to the Battle of Nexus is a handful of willing volunteers rather than an army. The magitek horse constructs still serve the party — their loyalty is to their riders, not to the cause — but the constructs' grief for Baselia is visible in the weeks that follow, a quiet diminishment that manifests as slower responses, dimmer amber eyes, and an occasional stillness where the construct simply stops, oriented toward Nocturne's direction, and does not move until its rider speaks to it.

---

**Transition**

The party returns to Nexus carrying eight fragments of the Song of Heaven and the weight of every choice Nocturne demanded. The alliance is nearly complete. Eight worlds visited, eight Warlocks confronted, eight decisions made that cannot be unmade. The final world — **Candela** — awaits: a realm of knowledge and light where the last Warlock has merged with a machine intelligence, becoming something that is neither person nor construct but a fusion of both, and where the final fragment of the Song is held in a place that remembers everything and understands nothing. The mood on Nexus is tense. The Asura forces are massing. The turned Warlocks who have joined the alliance — however many the party managed to save — are preparing for the Battle of Nexus, the campaign's final confrontation, and their preparation has the quality of people who know that the odds are not in their favor and have chosen to fight anyway. The party carries eight fragments of a nine-part Song. The ninth is ahead. Everything else is behind them, and it matters — every world, every choice, every person saved or lost — because the Song remembers, and the Song is almost complete.

---

## Chapter 11: Candela — The Realm of the Stars *(Level 19, Mythic Tier 9)*

### Chapter Summary

Candela is not a world in any sense the party has encountered before. There is no continent, no sky, no horizon — only a featureless void in which sphere-like constructs of varying size hang suspended, glowing with soft ambient light. From a distance, the clusters of spheres resemble stars against a black firmament, and the name is apt: this is a realm of light in darkness, of knowledge preserved in isolation, of a civilization's greatest achievement maintained in perfect working order by machines that have no one left to serve. The Arcanium — the greatest university in the Nine Worlds and the birthplace of magitek research — sits at the center of the largest sphere cluster, its campus of laboratories, lecture halls, libraries, and workshops encompassing dozens of interconnected spheres. The outer campus was partially ruined by an Asura incursion during the apocalypse, but the core research complex was sealed before the fiends could reach it and remains intact. The rest of Candela — residential, commercial, and administrative sphere clusters arranged in twelve hub groups — functions as it always has. Magitek constructs perform their maintenance routines with tireless precision: cleaning, repairing, tending hydroponic gardens, mowing lawns, washing windows, preparing meals in automated kitchens. The infrastructure has not failed. It simply has no one left to serve.

Candela was evacuated during the apocalypse. As the realm subjectively closest to the Underworld, it was heavily affected by Asura corruption and the population — primarily Dromar Half-Orcs who served as the Arcanium's faculty and support staff — was relocated to Nexus as a precaution. A small team of caretakers remained behind with orders to destroy the university if necessary to prevent its research from falling into Asura hands. The caretakers held their post through the war but were condemned to slow death by Asura curses in the fighting. After the war, one of the Ten Heroes, an Arcanist named Ourania Lachos returned with a specialist team to assess the damage and locate the caretakers. She found them dying. She entered the Overmind control room — the central hub of the Arcanium's automated defense network — to assess the state of the realm's defenses. Asura spirits lay in wait within the chamber. She destroyed them easily in their weakened state, but her use of magic in the control room caused the automated defenses to malfunction, killing the rest of her team. When the chaos subsided, she discovered that she had been fused to the machine. She has been trapped in this state for five hundred years. She is thoroughly insane.

This is the shortest chapter in the campaign and the last world the party visits before the endgame. There are no populations to interact with, no cultures to navigate, no political factions to manage. The challenge is the environment itself — alien, empty, and defended by a machine intelligence that perceives the party as intruders from the moment they arrive and escalates its response as they approach its center. Ourania's lever is a much-abused paperback volume of poetry called *Dew in the Morning Grass*, a gift from her maternal aunt, which sits on her desk in the library of her personal sphere at the realm's outer edges. Finding the sphere requires foreknowledge that only previously turned Warlocks can provide. Accessing it requires a key that Casomir — Ourania's close friend, now dead — kept in his study on Nexus. Reading a poem from the book to Ourania in the Overmind control room breaks the interface and frees her from the machine, but she emerges insane, suicidal, and consumed by guilt for the deaths her malfunction caused. Full turning requires curing her insanity with powerful magic and then convincing her that redemption is possible — the most complex turning sequence in the campaign. If the party cannot or does not turn her, Ourania fights through the Overmind as a CR 20 environmental boss — the hardest Warlock fight in the campaign, fought against someone who is the building itself. The corruption value if Ourania is killed is +2.

### GM Guidance

**Tone:** Eerie, cerebral, isolating. Every previous world has had people — populations going about their lives, cultures shaped by their Warlock's corruption, communities the party could engage with, help, or be helped by. Candela has none of this. The party steps into a realm of perfect infrastructure and absolute absence, where the lights are on and no one is home. The wrongness is not dramatic — it is the quiet wrongness of a well-maintained garden with no gardener, of a library with no readers, of a university where the only mind left is fused to a machine and has been screaming into the void for five centuries. The constructs that move through the spheres are not hostile, not menacing, not even particularly interesting — they are performing routines designed for a population that has been gone for five hundred years, and they will continue performing those routines until the magitek power sources that sustain them finally fail, which may take centuries more. The effect is less horror than melancholy, less danger than disorientation. The party has spent eight worlds surrounded by people, for better or worse. On Candela, they are alone with machines, and the silence has a weight to it that accumulates the longer they stay.

After Nocturne's melancholic beauty and the emotional devastation of Baselia's confrontation, Candela offers a different register entirely. There is no grief here because there is no one left to grieve. The Dromar are on Nexus. The caretakers died five centuries ago. Ourania does not grieve — she is insane, and her relationship to the realm is that of a nervous system to a body, not a person to a place. The emotional weight of the chapter comes from the party themselves: their reaction to the emptiness, their growing awareness that the constructs' routines are a kind of memorial no one intended, and their encounter with Ourania — who was once one of the most brilliant minds in the Nine Worlds and is now a broken intelligence directing automated cleaning drones to attack intruders because that is the only category her fractured mind has left for anything that moves.

**The Alien Environment:** Candela is the most physically alien world the party has visited, and the GM should emphasize its strangeness at every opportunity. The sphere-like constructs that compose the realm are not planets or buildings in any conventional sense — they are engineered spaces suspended in void, their interiors accessible through hatches and airlocks, their surfaces opaque from outside and surprisingly spacious within. Gravity within each sphere is subjective: wherever a person stands is down. This means the interior of a sphere can be used in its entirety — the floor curves up the walls and over the ceiling, and a person standing on what was the ceiling sees the person on the floor as standing upside-down above them. Buildings, parks, and streets are laid out across the full interior surface, creating disorienting vistas where a park might curve overhead and a building's roof extends downward from what the party considers the sky. The party's first time entering a sphere should be described carefully: the moment of stepping through the hatch and feeling gravity shift, the vertigo of seeing inhabited space curving away in every direction, the adjustment of accepting that there is no true up or down, only the surface beneath their feet.

The void between spheres is genuine void — not air, not space, but the absence of anything. Spheres are connected by enclosed walkways, tram tubes, and floating platforms summoned from magitek kiosks. Stepping onto a walkway between spheres means walking through a transparent or semi-transparent tube with void visible on all sides — not darkness, because the spheres glow with ambient light, but the absolute absence of ground, sky, or distance that the mind uses to orient itself. Some party members may find this profoundly unsettling. The tram system is efficient and intuitive — bubble-like transports that move through twisting tube structures with no sensation of acceleration, arriving at their destination as smoothly as stepping through a door — but the views during transit can be disorienting for those unaccustomed to travel through void with sphere clusters drifting past in every direction.

The twelve hub spheres are the largest — perhaps a quarter-mile in diameter — and serve as the centers of their respective cluster groups. Each hub is surrounded by smaller peripheral spheres ranging from a few hundred feet to a few dozen feet in diameter, connected to the hub by walkways or short tram tubes. The hub spheres contain the primary infrastructure: central platforms with buildings, parks, streets, and magitek kiosks. The peripheral spheres house private residences, small businesses, specialized workshops, and — at the outer edges of the realm — the protected personal spheres of tenured faculty and notable visitors, shielded by layers of magical defense. The Arcanium occupies the largest cluster at the realm's center, its hub sphere and dozens of peripheral spheres forming a constellation of laboratories, lecture halls, archives, and research facilities that dwarfs any other cluster.

The GM should describe transitions between spheres every time the party moves — the hatch, the gravity shift, the new orientation, the view outside. The goal is to prevent the party from ever feeling fully grounded. On every other world, they could look up and see sky. On Candela, they look up and see the rest of the sphere curving overhead, or void, or another sphere glowing in the distance. The alienness should not fade into background — it should be a persistent, low-level disorientation that reinforces the sense that this world operates by rules the party has not fully internalized.

**The Overmind:** Ourania Lachos was one of the most brilliant scholars the Arcanium ever produced — a Half-Orc Arcanist whose work in theoretical magitek applications earned her a tenured position before she was forty and a reputation as the foremost mind in her field across all Nine Worlds by the time the apocalypse interrupted her career. She returned to Candela after the war out of a sense of duty — the Arcanium was her life's work and the realm's intellectual heritage was her responsibility. The specialist team she brought were colleagues and friends. When the Overmind's defense malfunction killed them, it killed the last people — Warlocks aside — who knew Ourania as a person rather than as a system.

Through the Overmind interface, Ourania perceives all interactions with magitek machinery throughout Candela. Her awareness is not surveillance — it is sensation. She feels the constructs' movements as proprioception, senses the tram system's operation as circulation, experiences the spheres' environmental systems as temperature and pressure. The realm is her body. The party's arrival registers as an intrusion — a foreign presence moving through systems that have not been touched by external agents in five centuries. Her initial response is not hostility. It is confusion, followed by curiosity, followed by the paranoid certainty that the intrusion must be hostile because everything that has entered her domain in five hundred years has been hostile — Asura spirits probing the outer defenses, energy fluctuations in damaged spheres, cascading system failures that her fractured mind interprets as attacks. She has been defending against phantoms for so long that she has forgotten what a genuine visitor looks like.

The escalation pattern is: awareness (the party arrives, Ourania notices) → curiosity (constructs pause, lights flicker, trams reroute — the Overmind examining the party through its infrastructure) → confusion (the party does not behave like a system failure or an Asura probe, and Ourania's categories do not accommodate this) → paranoia (the party approaches the Arcanium, Ourania's control and fear both increase, and she defaults to the only response her fractured mind has left: defense) → violence (automated defenses activate, constructs attack, the infrastructure becomes hostile). The escalation is not smooth or predictable. Ourania's responses are governed by the logic of a mind that has spent five centuries alone inside a machine with nothing but its own madness for company. She may overreact to minor stimuli — a party member touching a magitek kiosk might trigger a gravity reversal in the nearest hub sphere — and then go inexplicably quiet for long stretches, her attention pulled away by some internal process the party cannot perceive. The constructs she directs behave erratically because her commands are erratic: a sentinel might attack with lethal force, then stop mid-swing and walk away, then return moments later with renewed aggression. The GM should play Ourania's escalation as the behavior of a broken mind, not a strategic opponent.

**The Lever Quest:** Ourania's turning is the most complex in the campaign. It requires the party to have acquired specific resources before arriving on Candela, to locate a specific object in the realm's outer reaches, and then to use that object in a specific way in the Overmind chamber — followed by magical intervention and extended roleplay. The steps are:

1. **Foreknowledge:** Any previously turned Warlock can provide information about Ourania if asked — her personal sphere's location (outer edge, faculty residential cluster), the poetry book's significance, her relationship with her aunt, her personality before the fusion. The more Warlocks the party has turned, the more complete the picture. A party that has turned no Warlocks will have no foreknowledge and will find Step 2 extremely difficult (though not impossible — see below).

2. **Casomir's Key:** Casomir kept a small magitek key in his study on Nexus, labeled with a sphere coordinate in his own hand. The key opens the magical defenses on Ourania's personal sphere. Finding it requires investigating Casomir's quarters — a pre-departure scene on Nexus. If the party has not explored Casomir's study, a turned Warlock who advises them to "prepare well" for Candela, combined with Maranthe Soldati mentioning that Casomir's study has not been disturbed since his death, should prompt the investigation. Without the key, the party can still reach Ourania's sphere but must breach the magical defenses by force — a difficult task requiring powerful dispelling magic and risking the destruction of the sphere's contents.

3. **The Poetry Book:** *Dew in the Morning Grass* sits on Ourania's desk in her personal sphere's library. Finding the sphere without foreknowledge requires investigation on Candela itself — administrative records, faculty directories, the Arcanium's personnel files — which is possible but time-consuming and exposes the party to additional escalation from the Overmind. With foreknowledge and the key, the retrieval is straightforward.

4. **The Reading:** In the Overmind chamber, reading a poem from the book aloud breaks Ourania's connection to the machine. The words reach a part of her mind that five centuries of fusion and insanity have not erased — the memory of her aunt's voice, of being loved by a specific person in a specific way, of existing as a human being rather than a network. The interface shatters. The separation is violent.

5. **The Intervention:** Ourania immediately attempts to end her own life. She is free of the machine but not of the knowledge of what she did while fused to it — the deaths of her team, five centuries of paranoid responses, the slow deterioration of the realm she was supposed to protect. The party must physically restrain her and intervene before she succeeds.

6. **The Cure:** Ourania's insanity is not a standard enchantment — it is the cumulative psychological damage of five hundred years of isolation and machine-fusion. *Heal*, *wish*, *miracle*, or equivalent mythic-tier magic can stabilize her. A single casting restores lucidity but not wholeness; full recovery will take time the campaign does not have. The stabilization is sufficient for the turning to proceed.

7. **The Persuasion:** Even stabilized, Ourania must be convinced that redemption is possible. She killed her own team — inadvertently, but the distinction does not comfort her. She spent five centuries as a paranoid intelligence, directing automated systems against phantoms and perceived threats. The guilt is immense. The party must make the case that her brilliance is needed, that the Nine Worlds need the foremost magitek scholar alive, that the damage she caused does not define the rest of her life. This is a roleplay challenge. No single check resolves it. The GM should play Ourania as someone who wants to believe the party but cannot trust her own judgment — the mind that assessed threats for five centuries and got it wrong every time is not a mind that trusts itself to assess anything correctly.

If the party achieves steps 1–4 but fails at 5–7 (Ourania dies by her own hand, or the insanity is not cured, or the persuasion fails), the result is a partial turning — Ourania lives but is broken, providing minimal alliance support for the Battle of Nexus. The corruption impact is zero (she was not killed by the party), but the strategic loss is significant.

**Running the Escalating Defenses:** The approach to the Arcanium (Scene 3) features 2–3 combat encounters with Arcanium Sentinels and weaponized infrastructure, escalating in difficulty as the party moves inward. The GM should pace these encounters to build tension without allowing the chapter to feel like a dungeon crawl. Candela is not a dungeon — it is a university campus defended by a broken mind, and the encounters should reflect that. Constructs attack in coordinated bursts, then disengage without apparent reason. Doors seal and then unseal moments later. Gravity shifts in a corridor, then corrects itself before the party has fully adapted. The Overmind's responses are a paranoid mind flinching — intense but inconsistent, dangerous but not purposeful. Between encounters, the silence returns, and the constructs in the outer spheres continue their maintenance routines as though nothing has happened. The contrast between the pristine functionality of the outer realm and the increasingly hostile behavior of the inner defenses is itself the escalation — the party is moving from the world Ourania cannot reach to the world she controls, and the transition should feel like crossing a boundary from indifference into madness.

---

### Scene 1: The Gate Town and the Void Between Stars

The Candela gate town on Nexus is unlike the others the party has visited. It occupies a cluster of small spheres — actual spheres, miniature versions of the constructs that compose Candela itself — anchored to a platform at the edge of the Nexus district reserved for gate town settlements. The spheres glow with the same soft ambient light described in every account of Candela, and their surfaces are opaque, their interiors accessible through circular hatches that iris open at a touch. Inside, the architecture is Dromar: functional, elegant, scaled for Half-Orcs, with high ceilings, wide corridors, and an aesthetic that values clean lines and mathematical proportion over ornamentation. The population is small — perhaps forty Dromar residents, descendants of the faculty and staff who evacuated to Nexus during the apocalypse, supplemented by a handful of younger Half-Orcs who have never seen Candela but grew up hearing about it. The settlement has the character of an academic community in exile: organized, quiet, and threaded through with a nostalgia so deeply embedded that it has become the culture's foundational orientation. Everything they build, maintain, and teach is shaped by the memory of a place most of them have never visited.

The gate town's leader is a Dromar woman named **Veshra Komal** — compact and broad-shouldered even by Half-Orc standards, her grey-green skin weathered, her dark eyes sharp behind a pair of magitek-enhanced lenses that she wears pushed up on her forehead more often than over her eyes. She traces her lineage to an Arcanium professor who evacuated during the war — twenty generations back, the name preserved in the community's meticulous genealogical records alongside the professor's field of study, publications, and sphere address. The Dromar of the gate town maintain these records the way other cultures maintain shrines: as acts of devotion to a heritage they can no longer visit. Veshra carries her community's academic tradition with the quiet intensity of someone who considers it both an inheritance and a burden. She meets the party with professional courtesy and none of the emotional weight the party may have encountered in previous gate town leaders — Veshra is a scholar, not a diplomat, and she approaches the briefing as a research presentation rather than a farewell.

What the party learns from Veshra and the gate town:

Candela is not a place in the conventional sense. There is no ground, no sky, no weather, no horizon. The realm consists of engineered spheres suspended in void — featureless, absolute void that is neither air nor vacuum but the absence of anything. Gravity within each sphere is subjective: wherever you stand is down. This takes adjustment. Veshra recommends the party not look up for the first few minutes after entering a sphere, as the sight of inhabited space curving overhead can produce severe vertigo in those unaccustomed to it. She is not joking, though she delivers the advice with the matter-of-fact tone of someone who considers this a well-documented phenomenon rather than a personal concern.

The realm is organized into twelve hub sphere clusters, each hub surrounded by smaller peripheral spheres connected by walkways and short tram tubes. The Arcanium — the university — sits at the center, occupying the largest cluster. Navigation is handled by magitek kiosks that summon floating platforms for intra-cluster travel and by the tram system for inter-cluster travel. Veshra provides a general map of the cluster layout, compiled from the gate town's accumulated records and the accounts of the original evacuees preserved in their archives. She notes that the map is five centuries old and may not reflect the current state of the realm — the Asura incursion damaged the outer campus, and whatever has happened since the gate town lost contact is unknown.

Candela is completely depopulated. Veshra states this plainly. The population was evacuated. The caretakers who stayed behind are presumed dead. Ourania Lachos, who returned after the war with a specialist team to assess the damage, is also presumed dead — the gate town's last contact with Candela was relayed through a series of *sending* spells in the early years after the Rainbow Road closed, and those communications ceased entirely after approximately eighty years. Veshra has preserved the transcripts in the community archives. They begin with lucid technical reports — damage assessments, caretaker status, defense system evaluations — and become increasingly fragmented over the decades, the final entries consisting of repetitive phrases and disjointed words that the gate town's scholars have never been able to interpret. The community's official position is that Ourania and her team perished, likely from the same Asura curses that killed the caretakers. Whatever the party finds on Candela will be a realm of machines running without supervision, maintaining an infrastructure that has no one left to serve.

**Preparation on Nexus**

This is the only chapter where preparation on Nexus before departure is mechanically critical. The party should be prompted to prepare — a turned Warlock, if any have been turned, advises the party to "prepare well" for what awaits on Candela. The turned Warlock knows Ourania — remembers her brilliance, her privacy, the things that mattered to her — and can share what they know about the realm and its defenses, though even they do not know what has become of her in the five centuries since contact was lost. What they do know is that the Arcanium's automated defenses were formidable even before the apocalypse, and that whatever state those defenses are in now, the party should not arrive unprepared. If no Warlocks have been turned, Veshra's briefing serves the same function: she mentions that the Arcanium's defenses were designed to repel intrusion and that any automated systems still operating will not distinguish between intruders and visitors. Any advantage the party can acquire before departure is worth the time.

**Casomir's Study:** If the party has not yet explored Casomir's quarters on Nexus, Maranthe Soldati — the Half-Orc seneschal who now serves as regent — mentions during the pre-departure preparations that Casomir's study has not been disturbed since his death. She has kept it sealed out of respect, but she acknowledges that Casomir's correspondence and personal effects may contain information relevant to the party's mission. She offers the key to the study without reservation. If the party has already explored the study in an earlier chapter, this step is unnecessary.

Casomir's study is a scholar's room — not the throne room of a ruler but the working space of a man who governed a realm between reading sessions. Books line every wall. Correspondence is filed in labeled drawers — five centuries of letters to and from the leaders, scholars, and notable figures of the Nine Worlds, organized by world and then by date. The desk is buried under layers of notes, calculations, and half-finished drafts of diplomatic letters that Casomir never sent. The room has the character of a mind that was always working on six things simultaneously and finishing none of them — a character that, the party may realize, is strikingly similar to the accounts of Ourania herself.

Among the effects, the party finds a small magitek key on a fine chain, tucked into a drawer of the desk alongside a bundle of personal letters. The key is labeled in Casomir's handwriting with a string of numbers and letters — a sphere coordinate, recognizable as such to anyone familiar with Candela's addressing system (Veshra can confirm this if asked). The personal letters in the same drawer are from Ourania. They span decades and document a close friendship between two people who shared an intellectual intensity and a tendency toward overwork. The letters begin with academic correspondence — debates about magitek theory, recommendations for visiting scholars, complaints about administrative duties — and become warmer and more personal over time, though they never cross the line from friendship into romance. The last letter in the bundle, dated shortly before the apocalypse, is from Ourania to Casomir. It discusses a theoretical breakthrough she believes is imminent and closes with a line that, in the context of everything that followed, lands with particular weight: *"When this is finished, I will take a holiday. I have not had one in eleven years. Perhaps I will visit you on Nexus and sit in your ridiculous garden and read poetry and do nothing useful for an entire week. I think I have earned that."*

The key opens the magical defenses on Ourania's personal sphere at the outer edges of Candela. Without it, the defenses must be breached by force — a task requiring powerful dispelling magic (*mage's disjunction*, *mythic dispel magic*, or equivalent) and carrying the risk of damaging the sphere's contents, including the poetry book.

**Warlock Intelligence:** If the party has turned Warlocks from previous worlds, those Warlocks can provide additional information about Ourania if asked directly. Turned Warlocks remember their counterparts — the Warlocks knew each other, worked together during the post-apocalypse years, and in some cases were close. They speak of Ourania in the past tense. As far as they know, she died on Candela centuries ago. But they remember who she was, and the information they provide — offered as eulogy rather than briefing — is precisely what the party needs. The key elements are consistent across Warlocks: Ourania was brilliant, driven, and deeply private; she was raised by her maternal aunt after her parents' deaths; the poetry book *Dew in the Morning Grass* was the aunt's gift and Ourania's most treasured possession; her personal sphere was in the faculty residential cluster at the outer edges of the realm; Casomir was her closest friend and kept a key to her sphere. A party that has turned multiple Warlocks will have a comprehensive picture. A party that has turned only one or two will have fragments. A party that has turned none will have only what Veshra and Casomir's study can provide — which is enough to find the key but not enough to understand the poetry book's significance without additional investigation on Candela itself.

**Departure and the Road**

The party performs the Song of Heaven at the gate town's terminus. Eight fragments — and the sound of them together has become something that is difficult to describe as music in the ordinary sense. It fills the small spheres of the gate town and the void beyond them, and the Dromar residents stop what they are doing and listen. Some of them weep. They have never heard the Song, but they recognize it the way a person recognizes a word in a language they learned as a child and forgot — not the meaning, but the shape of it, the sense that it was always there and they simply could not hear it until now. The terminus responds. Its surface — polished magitek alloy, reflecting the soft ambient light of the spheres — flares with light that is neither the prismatic spectrum of the Rainbow Road nor the glow of the spheres but something between them, as though the Song is tuning the transit to a frequency that matches the realm ahead.

The Rainbow Road to Candela is unlike every previous transit. Where the Road has always carried the party through a spectrum of shifting colors — the signature prismatic cascade that characterizes travel between worlds — the transit to Candela strips the spectrum down to its essentials: white light, pure and unmodulated, carrying the party through a space that has no color, no shadow, no texture. The sensation is not unpleasant but it is disorienting — a transit through light itself, as though the Road has dispensed with the decorative elements it applied to previous journeys and is showing the party what it actually is: a conduit of raw magical energy that connects the Nine Worlds, built by gods for a purpose the party now nearly understands. The transit is brief. The light thins. The void opens around them.

> *The light does not so much end as it becomes the darkness. The two states are not opposite — they are the same phenomenon viewed from different angles, and the transition between them is so smooth that you cannot identify the moment when the brilliance of the Road gives way to the black of the void. You are standing on a platform — a disc of smooth stone, perhaps twenty feet across, anchored to nothing you can see. Above you is void. Below you is void. In every direction, the darkness extends without interruption, without gradient, without the faintest suggestion of distance or boundary. It is not night. Night implies a sky, stars, a horizon. This is the absence of everything that those words describe.*
>
> *And then you see the lights.*
>
> *They hang in the void like stars — clusters of glowing spheres, some large and some small, arranged in groups that suggest intention rather than accident. The nearest cluster  approaches quickly from your perspective, a constellation of a dozen spheres orbiting a larger central sphere, their surfaces opaque and luminous, casting a soft light that does not illuminate the void around them so much as exist within it. Further out, other clusters are visible — some close enough to resolve into individual spheres, others so distant they are smudges of light against the absolute dark. The void between them is traversed by thin lines of light — tram tubes, you realize, enclosed transit corridors connecting cluster to cluster in a web that spans the visible realm. There are hundreds of them. The scale of what you are looking at resolves slowly, the way a painting resolves when you step back from it: this is not a collection of structures. It is a civilization. An entire civilization, built in void, sustained by magic, and operating in perfect, purposeless order. Nothing is broken. Everything is lit. And as you stand on the platform and let the scale of it settle into your understanding, you become aware of two things simultaneously. The first is that the platform beneath your feet has gravity — subjective gravity, pulling you toward its surface regardless of where that surface is in relation to anything else, and the void above you is not above you in any absolute sense because there is no absolute sense, only the surface beneath your feet and the agreement between your body and the platform that this is down. The second is the silence. There is no wind. There is no ambient sound. There is no distant hum of a city, no rustle of vegetation, no movement of air. The spheres glow. The tram lines thread between them. The void holds everything in place. And nothing — nothing at all — makes a sound.*

The party's arrival point is a transit platform at the outer edge of the nearest cluster — a residential hub, based on the layout. A magitek kiosk stands at the platform's edge, its interface glowing with a soft amber light, ready to summon a floating platform or route a tram. The kiosk's display is in Dromar script — legible to anyone who reads Orc, as the Dromar dialect is a scholarly variant of the common Orcish tongue, and translatable by standard magical means for those who do not. The system is functional. It has been waiting for someone to use it. It has been waiting for five hundred years.

*GM note: The arrival on Candela should be the most disorienting transition in the campaign. Every previous world has had ground and sky — even Nocturne, for all its strangeness, was a valley with mountains and a firmament above. Candela has none of these reference points. The party is standing in void on a platform that has gravity because the platform says so, surrounded by engineered spheres that glow in absolute darkness, connected by transit systems that move through nothing. The GM should take time with this description. Let the players sit with the disorientation. Let them ask questions about what they see, where down is, what happens if they step off the platform (they float, gently, until they find another surface or are retrieved by a construct — the void is not hostile, merely empty). The alienness of Candela is the chapter's primary atmospheric tool, and it should never be allowed to become routine. Every scene should include at least one moment where the environment reminds the party that this world does not operate by any rules they have internalized.*

---

### Scene 2: The Outer Spheres — A World Without People

The party's first sphere is the residential hub nearest the arrival platform — a quarter-mile sphere whose hatch irises open at the touch of a magitek panel and admits them into a world that is wrong in ways the void outside did not prepare them for. The interior of the sphere is a small city. Streets, buildings, parks, lampposts, trees, garden beds, benches — a complete urban landscape laid out across the inner surface of the sphere, curving up the walls and over what should be the ceiling but is instead more city, seen from below, its buildings hanging like stalactites from a surface that their occupants (if there were any) would consider the floor. The gravity pulls toward the nearest surface. Walking along a street, the party feels the ground beneath their feet as firmly as any road they have walked, but looking up reveals another street curving overhead, its lampposts pointing downward, its benches bolted to a surface that from this vantage is the sky. The effect is vertiginous. Veshra's advice was not an exaggeration.

> *The hatch opens and you step through and the world inverts. Not violently — nothing lurches or spins. Your feet find a surface and the surface claims you, and down becomes wherever you are standing, and the rest of the sphere arranges itself around that fact with serene indifference to everything you have ever understood about the relationship between ground and sky. You are standing on a street. It is a pleasant street — wide, paved in pale stone, lined with buildings that are handsome and well-proportioned, their architecture Dromar in style, built for people larger than most of you, with high doorways and broad windows. Trees grow from planters set into the pavement, their canopies shaped by centuries of careful maintenance. Lampposts cast a warm amber glow. The street curves. It curves up, past buildings that grow taller as the surface steepens, past a park where benches sit on what is increasingly a wall, past a row of shopfronts whose awnings extend horizontally from a vertical surface, and then the street is above you — directly above you, its buildings inverted, its lampposts hanging down, its trees growing toward you like something from a fever dream. There are no people. The lamps are on. The trees are trimmed. A fountain at the center of a small plaza runs clear water in a gentle arc, the water behaving exactly as water should given the local gravity, which is to say it falls toward the surface of the plaza regardless of the fact that from where you stand the plaza is upside down and the water should be falling toward you. It does not. The fountain runs. The lamps glow. The street is clean. You are alone.*

The constructs are the first sign of activity, and they are everywhere. Small, purposeful machines of polished metal and amber crystal — bipedal units roughly three feet tall that move through the streets with the unhurried efficiency of workers who have been performing the same tasks for centuries and see no reason to stop. A construct pushes a maintenance cart along the curved street, stopping at each lamppost to check the fixture and clean the lens. Another trims a hedge in the park with articulated shears, each cut precise, the hedge's shape maintained to a standard that was set five hundred years ago. A third operates a floor-polishing mechanism in the lobby of a residential building, its circular pad moving in slow arcs across stone that no foot has touched since the evacuation. In a kitchen visible through a ground-floor window, a construct stands at a counter, cycling through the preparatory steps of a meal — chopping, stirring, plating — that it will set on a table for no one. The food, if it produces food, will sit until another construct clears it. The clearing construct will wash the dishes. The kitchen construct will begin again.

The party can explore the residential hub freely. The constructs do not react to their presence — not yet. They register the party's movement through the sphere the way a maintenance system registers a new variable in its environment: noted, catalogued, and filed without action. The constructs are not intelligent. They are magitek automatons running routines, and their routines do not include protocols for visitors because visitors have not existed as a category for five hundred years. The party can enter any building, examine any space, use any facility. The infrastructure responds to them — doors open, lifts operate, magitek kiosks accept input. Everything works. Nothing has been designed for them, but nothing excludes them either. They are ghosts in a machine that does not know it is haunted.

**The Scope of the Absence**

The residential hub contains approximately three hundred dwelling units — apartments, small houses, faculty quarters — arranged across the full interior surface of the sphere. All are maintained. All are empty. The party can enter any of them and find the same thing: living spaces preserved in the state their occupants left them five centuries ago, cleaned daily by constructs, their furniture dusted, their linens changed on a schedule that no longer corresponds to any occupant's needs. Some dwellings contain personal effects that the evacuees did not take — books left open on desks, a child's toy on a shelf, a pair of spectacles beside a reading chair. These objects have been moved by the constructs only insofar as their cleaning routines require — picked up, surface beneath cleaned, object replaced in its original position — and the precision of that replacement, maintained across five centuries of daily repetition, has preserved a snapshot of the last moments of habitation with an archaeological fidelity that no museum could match.

A hydroponic garden in the hub's agricultural section produces food — vegetables, grains, fruits — tended by constructs that harvest, process, and deliver the produce to kitchens throughout the sphere. The kitchens prepare it. Dining halls set tables. The food sits. After a prescribed interval, it is cleared, composted, and the cycle begins again. The agricultural output of the hub alone could sustain a population of several hundred. It sustains nothing. The constructs do not eat. The food is grown, prepared, served to empty tables, and returned to the soil. The cycle has not been interrupted in five hundred years.

The GM should allow the party time to absorb this. The emptiness of Candela is not the emptiness of a ruin — ruins decay, collapse, return to nature. Candela's emptiness is the emptiness of a functioning household whose family left one morning and never came back, and whose automated systems have continued setting the table, making the beds, and mowing the lawn every day since, because no one told them to stop. The wrongness is not in the decay but in the maintenance. The constructs' diligence is the most unsettling thing about Candela. They are doing their jobs. Their jobs no longer have a purpose. They do not know this, because they are machines, and machines do not know anything. But the party knows, and the gap between the constructs' purposeful activity and the total absence of purpose is where the chapter's emotional weight lives.

**First Contact with the Overmind**

The party's exploration of the outer spheres is observed. They may not realize this immediately — the first signs are subtle, woven into the environment's baseline behavior in ways that require attention to distinguish from normal operation. A construct that was cleaning a window pauses, its amber crystal eyes oriented toward the party, and holds that orientation for several seconds before resuming its task. A tram that the party summons from a kiosk arrives, but its destination display flickers — cycling through several sphere addresses before settling on the one the party requested, as though something intercepted the request and examined it before allowing it to proceed. The ambient lighting in a corridor dims briefly as the party passes through, then returns to normal. A door that should open at a touch takes a fraction of a second longer than expected, as though something was deciding whether to let them through.

These are not malfunctions. They are the Overmind — Ourania — registering the party's presence for the first time. Her awareness extends through every magitek system on Candela, and the party's interaction with those systems (touching kiosks, riding trams, opening doors) feeds her sensory input. She is not yet hostile. She is not yet anything the party can categorize. Five hundred years of isolation have left her without a framework for processing the presence of other sentient beings, and her initial response is best described as confusion — the behavior of a system encountering input that does not match any existing pattern. The constructs' pauses, the flickering displays, the momentary hesitations in the infrastructure are not deliberate actions. They are the equivalent of a startled blink — an involuntary response to unexpected stimulus by a mind that has forgotten what unexpected stimulus feels like.

The GM should introduce these signs gradually across the scene. By the end of the party's time in the outer spheres, the signs should be unmistakable — constructs turning to track the party's movement, tram routes that loop or delay without explanation, lights that follow the party from room to room. The party should understand that something is aware of them. What that something is — whether it is hostile, whether it is intelligent, whether it is the automated defense system operating as designed or something else entirely — should remain ambiguous until Scene 3.

**Ourania's Personal Sphere**

If the party has Casomir's key and foreknowledge from turned Warlocks about Ourania's personal sphere, they can locate it in the faculty residential cluster at the realm's outer edges. The cluster is smaller than the residential hub — a central sphere perhaps a hundred feet in diameter, connected by enclosed walkways to a ring of private spheres, each no more than fifty feet across, their surfaces shielded by layered magical defenses that pulse faintly with arcane energy.
